cards.front: What is Goodsall's rule for fistula-in-ano?
cards.back:
Fistulas with an external opening anterior to a transverse line through the anus track in a straight line to the dentate line (straight anterior course). Fistulas posterior to this transverse line curve and open in the posterior midline at the dentate line (curved course).

Goodsall's rule helps predict the internal opening of an anorectal fistula, guiding surgical planning. Understanding the anatomy is critical to avoid sphincter injury during repair.

cards.front: What is the primary surgical treatment for a low-lying fistula-in-ano (not involving the external sphincter)?
cards.back:
Primary fistulotomy: unroofing the tract from external to internal opening, allowing healing by secondary intention.

Fistulotomy is curative for low-lying fistulas that do not involve the external sphincter. High-lying fistulas involving the external sphincter require staged procedures with a Seton suture to avoid fecal incontinence.

cards.front: What is the LIFT procedure for fistula-in-ano?
cards.back:
Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract (LIFT): accesses the fistula between the internal and external sphincter muscles, ligating the tract while sparing the sphincters.

LIFT is used for complex fistulas to preserve sphincter function, thereby reducing the risk of fecal incontinence. It is part of the sphincter-sparing approach for high transsphincteric fistulas.

cards.front: What is the role of a Seton suture in treating high-lying fistula-in-ano?
cards.back:
A Seton (rubber band or suture) is placed through the fistula tract involving the external sphincter. It promotes drainage and fibrosis, delineates anatomy, and reduces the incidence of incontinence by staged division of the sphincter.

High fistulas involving the external sphincter cannot be fully unroofed without causing fecal incontinence. The Seton slowly cuts through the sphincter over time, allowing fibrosis that maintains continence.

cards.front: What is the definition of pilonidal disease?
cards.back:
A cyst or abscess near/on the intergluteal cleft of the sacrococcygeal area, containing hair and skin debris. It results from obstruction of hair follicles in that area.

Pilonidal means 'nest of hair' (pilo = hair, nidal = nest). It is associated with prolonged sitting, obesity, and high body hair density. Most common in young men aged 15-35.

cards.front: What percentage of pilonidal abscesses treated with I&D develop chronic pilonidal sinuses?
cards.back:
40%

Simple I&D is effective for acute infection but has a high recurrence rate. Surgical excision (pilonidal cystotomy) is indicated for failure of healing, recurrent disease, or complex disease.

cards.front: Describe the two types of rectal prolapse.
cards.back:
1. False/partial/mucosal prolapse: only the mucosa protrudes; shows radial furrows; most common in childhood.
2. True/complete prolapse: full-thickness extrusion of rectal wall; shows concentric folds. Graded 1st (includes mucocutaneous junction), 2nd (without mucocutaneous junction), or 3rd degree (internal/occult intussusception).

Distinguishing true from false prolapse affects management. True prolapse is most common overall and more common in women >50 years. False prolapse can mimic hemorrhoids.

cards.front: What are the risk factors for rectal prolapse?
cards.back:
Gynecological surgery, chronic neurologic/psychiatric disorders affecting motility (e.g., chronic constipation), multiparity, and weak pelvic floor.

Rectal prolapse affects extremes of age (<5 yr and >50 yr) and predominantly women (85%). Pelvic floor weakness and chronic straining are key predisposing factors.

cards.front: What is the most common tumour of the anal canal, and how is it treated?
cards.back:
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) accounts for 75% of anal canal tumours. Treatment is chemoradiation (for most cases). Surgery (local excision) is reserved for very early lesions; salvage APR (abdominoperineal resection) for chemoradiation failures.

SCC of the anal canal is strongly associated with HPV infection. High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) is a precursor. 5-year survival is 80% with chemoradiation.

cards.front: What is the prognosis of anal canal malignant melanoma?
cards.back:
Less than 5% 5-year survival. It is the 3rd most common site for primary malignant melanoma (after skin and eyes), with aggressive behavior and frequent distant metastases at diagnosis.

Anal melanoma is often diagnosed late due to non-specific symptoms (bleeding, mass, pain, change in bowel habits). Only one-third are pigmented. Treatment is wide local excision or APR, but prognosis remains very poor.

cards.front: What are the key features of simple hepatic cysts?
cards.back:
Form from biliary ducts that do not communicate with the intrahepatic biliary tree; contain clear fluid. Usually asymptomatic. Always benign. Diagnosed by U/S (well-demarcated, non-enhancing on CT). Treatment only if >4 cm or symptomatic: laparoscopic/open cyst wall removal (unroofing).

Simple hepatic cysts are the most common type. They must be distinguished from cystadenoma (premalignant), echinococcal cyst, and polycystic liver disease based on imaging characteristics and clinical context.

cards.front: What is the association between polycystic liver disease (PCLD) and renal disease?
cards.back:
50% of PCLD patients over age 60 have associated polycystic kidney disease. PCLD is most commonly an extra-renal manifestation of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).

PCLD features >20 cysts replacing much of the liver parenchyma. It is more common in females and is typically asymptomatic until the cyst-to-parenchyma ratio exceeds 1, causing mass-effect symptoms.

cards.front: What are the clinical complications of choledochal cysts?
cards.back:
Recurrent abdominal pain, intermittent jaundice, symptomatic gallstones, pancreatitis, portal hypertension, biliary cirrhosis, cyst rupture, and significantly increased risk of biliary malignancy (cholangiocarcinoma).

Choledochal cysts are congenital malformations of the bile ducts classified by the Todani system. Majority present before age 10. Complete excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticoenterostomy is the treatment; malignancy risk mandates excision.

cards.front: What is hydatid (cystic echinococcosis) disease of the liver, and what is the treatment?
cards.back:
Infection by Echinococcus granulosus parasite through ingestion of eggs (exposure to dogs, sheep, cattle, etc.). Larvae enter blood/lymph and form hepatic cysts. Treatment: albendazole (anti-helminthic, up to 30% cure), surgical pericystectomy/hepatectomy, or percutaneous PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, re-aspiration). Cyst rupture can cause anaphylaxis.

Hydatid disease is common in Southern Europe, Middle East, Australasia, and South America. Cyst rupture is dangerous, causing anaphylaxis, eosinophilia, and dissemination. Pre-operative albendazole is given to reduce risk of recurrence.

cards.front: What distinguishes cystadenoma from other liver cysts, and what is the management?
cards.back:
Cystadenoma is a rare premalignant cystic neoplasm of the bile ducts. On U/S: anechoic mass with internal septations that are highly echogenic. All complex multiloculated liver cysts (except echinococcal) should be excised due to malignancy risk. Cystadenocarcinoma is the malignant counterpart.

Cystadenomas are the most common premalignant liver lesion. They are differentiated from simple cysts by the presence of septations and echogenic content. Elevated CEA and CA19-9 may suggest malignant transformation.

cards.front: What are the most common organisms in pyogenic liver abscess?
cards.back:
Most often polymicrobial: Klebsiella, E. coli, Proteus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and anaerobes.

Pyogenic liver abscess is the most common type of liver abscess. Sources include direct spread from biliary tract, portal spread from GI infection, systemic infection (e.g., endocarditis), or direct inoculation. Treatment: prolonged antibiotics (>6 weeks) and percutaneous/surgical drainage.

cards.front: What antibiotic regimen is used to treat a pyogenic liver abscess?
cards.back:
Prolonged antibiotic therapy for >6 weeks: ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam, combined with U/S- or CT-guided percutaneous drainage.

The goal of treatment is to treat the underlying cause (e.g., biliary source), provide adequate drainage, and eradicate infection. Overall mortality is 15%, with higher rates in elderly, multi-organ failure, and immunocompromised patients.

cards.front: What are the imaging characteristics of a cavernous hemangioma of the liver on CT and MRI?
cards.back:
CT: well-demarcated hypodense mass with peripheral enhancement on arterial phase and centripetal (fill-in) enhancement on delayed phases. U/S: homogeneous hyperechoic mass. MRI is also used. Biopsy should be avoided due to hemorrhage risk.

Hemangioma is the most common benign hepatic tumour (M:F = 3:1). Usually small and asymptomatic; giant hemangiomas (>10 cm) can cause abdominal discomfort or consumptive coagulopathy in children. Treatment is only for symptomatic cases.

cards.front: What is focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) and how is it distinguished on imaging?
cards.back:
FNH is a benign hyperplastic response to a vascular anomaly in the liver. Classic CT finding: central stellate scar surrounded by a homogeneous enhancing lesion. No malignant potential. Confirmed FNH requires no treatment. More common in females of reproductive age.

FNH must be differentiated from hepatic adenoma (which has malignant potential and risk of rupture) and fibrolamellar HCC. MRI and biopsy may be required. Once confirmed as FNH, no further treatment or surveillance is needed.

cards.front: What are the risk factors and indications for excision of hepatic adenoma?
cards.back:
Risk factors: female, ages 20-50, estrogen use (OCP, pregnancy), metabolic syndrome, anabolic steroids, type 1 glycogen storage disease. Indications for excision: size >5 cm or symptomatic in women; any size in men (due to higher risk of transformation to HCC and spontaneous rupture).

Hepatic adenoma is a benign abnormal growth of glandular epithelium. Stop offending agents (OCP, steroids). Risk of transformation to HCC and spontaneous rupture/hemorrhage drives surgical management, especially in men.

cards.front: What are the risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)?
cards.back:
Chronic liver inflammation/cirrhosis from any cause, chronic hepatitis B (inherently oncogenic) and hepatitis C, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, NASH, OCPs and anabolic steroids, smoking, alcohol, betel nut chewing, and chemical carcinogens (aflatoxin, microcystin, vinyl chloride — vinyl chloride is associated with angiosarcoma).

HCC is the most common primary liver cancer. The key distinction is that hepatitis B can cause HCC without cirrhosis (inherently oncogenic), while hepatitis C causes HCC only in the setting of cirrhosis.

cards.front: What tumour marker is elevated in approximately 80% of HCC patients, and what does a triphasic CT show?
cards.back:
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated in ~80% of HCC patients. Triphasic CT shows: enhancement on arterial phase with washout on portal venous phase (pathognomonic pattern for HCC).

The arterial enhancement and venous washout pattern on triphasic CT is characteristic of HCC and can allow diagnosis without biopsy in appropriate clinical settings. ALP, bilirubin, and AFP are the key labs.

cards.front: What are the Milan Criteria for liver transplantation in HCC?
cards.back:
Single tumour ≤5 cm, OR up to 3 tumours each ≤3 cm, with no macrovascular invasion and no extrahepatic disease.

Milan Criteria are the most widely used transplant criteria for HCC. The UCSF criteria are more liberal (single tumour <6.5 cm, or up to 3 tumours each <4.5 cm, total diameter <8 cm). Toronto Criteria have no tumour size or number restrictions.

cards.front: What is the 5-year survival for HCC following complete surgical resection?
cards.back:
40-70% after complete resection. Overall 5-year survival for all HCC patients is 18%.

Only about 10% of HCC patients have resectable tumours due to associated cirrhosis limiting hepatic reserve. Non-surgical options include TACE, RFA, percutaneous ethanol injection, and sorafenib for systemic therapy.

cards.front: What is the Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) score used for, and what does it assess?
cards.back:
The CTP score estimates prognosis in liver disease and helps determine operative risk. It assesses: bilirubin, albumin, INR/PT, presence/severity of ascites, and grade of hepatic encephalopathy. Class A (5-6): best prognosis; Class B (7-9): intermediate; Class C (10-15): worst prognosis.

CTP Class A has ~85% 1-year survival, Class B ~57%, Class C ~35%. Cirrhosis is a relative contraindication to tumour resection due to decreased hepatic reserve, making CTP scoring critical for surgical planning.

cards.front: What are the most common sources of secondary (metastatic) liver disease, and what is the treatment for colorectal liver metastases?
cards.back:
Most common primary sites: colorectal (most common), lung, breast, pancreas, GI NET, melanoma, ovary, uterus, kidney, and gallbladder. For colorectal metastases: hepatic resection combined with chemotherapy is standard of care if complete resection of primary and metastases is possible; 5-year survival 30-60%.

Secondary liver metastases are the most common malignant liver tumour. Their presence indicates Stage IV disease. Colorectal liver metastases are unique in that resection provides the greatest chance of cure among all metastatic cancers.

cards.front: What is the MELD score and how is it used in liver transplantation?
cards.back:
Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) estimates 3-month survival following TIPS and is used to prioritize patients awaiting liver transplant. It is based on: creatinine, bilirubin, INR, sodium (MELD-Na), female sex, and serum albumin. Higher MELD score = higher priority for transplant allocation.

MELD replaced the CTP score for organ allocation in Canada and the US. It is an objective, continuous score that correlates with mortality risk while awaiting transplant.

cards.front: What are the absolute contraindications to liver transplantation?
cards.back:
Active alcohol/substance use, extrahepatic malignancy within 5 years, advanced cardiopulmonary disease, and active uncontrolled infection.

Liver transplant is indicated for decompensated cirrhosis, unresectable primary liver cancers, acute liver failure, and liver-based metabolic conditions. Contraindications ensure appropriate patient selection given the scarcity of donor organs.

cards.front: What are the post-liver transplant complications and what is the leading cause of mortality?
cards.back:
Complications include: primary non-function (requires urgent re-transplantation), acute/chronic rejection, ischemia-reperfusion injury, vascular complications (hepatic artery or portal vein thrombosis, IVC obstruction), biliary complications (fever, increasing bilirubin and ALP), and immunosuppression-related issues (HTN, renal disease, DM, malignancy). Leading cause of post-transplant mortality: infection.

Immunosuppression is life-saving for graft survival but creates vulnerability to opportunistic infections. One-year patient survival is ~85%, with graft survival >80% at 1 year and 60-70% at 5 years.

cards.front: What are the risk factors for cholesterol gallstones (the classic 4 F's)?
cards.back:
The 4 F's: Fat (obesity), Female, Fertile (multiparity/estrogen use), and Forties (increasing age >40). Additional factors include impaired gallbladder emptying (DM, TPN, starvation), rapid weight loss, and OCP use.

Cholesterol stones make up 80% of gallstones in North America. They form due to an imbalance between cholesterol and its solubilizing agents (bile salts and lecithin), leading to cholesterol supersaturation and precipitation.

cards.front: What conditions predispose to pigment gallstone formation?
cards.back:
Black pigment stones: conditions increasing systemic bilirubin — chronic hemolytic anemias (especially sickle cell disease), ineffective erythropoiesis, ileal disease, extended ileal resection, and liver cirrhosis. Brown pigment stones: bile stasis from obstruction and biliary infection (especially E. coli).

Pigment stones (calcium bilirubinate) account for 20% of gallstones in North America. Understanding the distinction between black and brown pigment stones is clinically relevant for identifying the underlying cause.

cards.front: What is the diagnostic procedure of choice for cholelithiasis, and what is its specificity?
cards.back:
Ultrasound (U/S) is the diagnostic procedure of choice; 95% specific for detecting gallstones.

U/S is non-invasive, inexpensive, and reliable for gallstones. It images for signs of inflammation, obstruction, and stone localization. Normal bloodwork (CBC, LFTs, bilirubin, lipase) is expected in uncomplicated cholelithiasis.

cards.front: How does biliary colic differ clinically from acute cholecystitis?
cards.back:
Biliary colic: transient gallstone impaction in the cystic duct without infection; steady, severe dull pain for minutes to hours (<6 h), crescendo-decrescendo pattern, no peritoneal findings, no systemic signs, normal bloodwork. Acute cholecystitis: sustained impaction causing inflammation; constant pain >6 h, fever, Murphy's sign, elevated WBC, requires antibiotics and cholecystectomy.

The key distinction is that biliary colic pain resolves (stone dislodges) and has no peritoneal signs, while cholecystitis pain is constant with local peritoneal findings (Murphy's sign). Biliary colic is managed with analgesia and elective cholecystectomy.

cards.front: What is Murphy's sign, and in which condition is it found?
cards.back:
Murphy's sign: arrest of inspiration when the examiner's fingers are pressed deeply beneath the right costal margin. It occurs in acute cholecystitis when the inflamed gallbladder descends and contacts the examiner's fingers causing pain. Sonographic Murphy's sign is the U/S equivalent.

Murphy's sign is a classic finding of acute cholecystitis. U/S has 98% sensitivity for cholecystitis; HIDA scan is used if U/S is negative. Signs on U/S include gallbladder wall thickening >4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and sonographic Murphy's sign.

cards.front: What are the complications of acute cholecystitis?
cards.back:
Gangrenous gallbladder (20%, most common), perforation (may cause abscess or local peritonitis), Mirizzi syndrome, empyema (suppurative cholecystitis), emphysematous cholecystitis (gas in gallbladder wall; risk in diabetics), and cholecystoenteric fistula (may lead to gallstone ileus).

Emphysematous cholecystitis from gas-forming organisms (C. welchii, E. coli, Klebsiella) is particularly dangerous in diabetic patients and requires urgent surgery. Gangrenous cholecystitis indicates ischemic necrosis and is the most common complication.

cards.front: What is the Critical View of Safety (CVS) in laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
cards.back:
CVS requires three criteria before clipping the cystic duct and artery: 1) The hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue; 2) The lower one-third of the gallbladder is dissected free from the liver bed; 3) Only two structures (cystic duct and cystic artery) are seen entering the gallbladder.

CVS is the standard safety measure to reduce CBD injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. CBD injury occurs in 0.3-0.5% of cases. Rouviere's sulcus (fissure between right lobe and caudate) is a useful landmark to keep dissection anterior to.

cards.front: When is intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) indicated during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
cards.back:
Indications for IOC: clarify bile duct anatomy, history of biliary pancreatitis, small gallstones with a wide cystic duct (>15 mm), and jaundice. IOC has largely been replaced by preoperative MRCP.

IOC involves injection of radiographic contrast into the cystic duct during laparoscopic cholecystectomy to identify CBD stones, clarify biliary anatomy, and prevent CBD injury. MRCP provides equivalent information non-invasively pre-operatively.

cards.front: What is acalculous cholecystitis, and who is at risk?
cards.back:
Acute or chronic cholecystitis in the absence of gallstones, typically due to gallbladder ischemia and stasis. Occurs in 10% of acute cholecystitis cases. Risk factors: ICU admission (most common), DM, immunosuppression, trauma, TPN, and sepsis.

Acalculous cholecystitis is seen in critically ill patients. HIDA scan is the most useful confirming study (non-filling gallbladder). Management is IV antibiotics and cholecystectomy (or percutaneous cholecystostomy if unstable).

cards.front: What is choledocholithiasis, and what imaging is the non-invasive diagnostic test of choice?
cards.back:
Choledocholithiasis is the presence of stones in the common bile duct (CBD). Clinically: RUQ tenderness, acholic stool, dark urine, and fluctuating jaundice. MRCP (90% sensitive) is the non-invasive diagnostic test of choice for visualizing the ampullary region and biliary/pancreatic anatomy.

Secondary CBD stones are the most common form (85%), arising from the gallbladder. ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic for CBD stones but carries risks of pancreatitis (1-2%) and biliary sepsis. MRCP avoids these risks for initial diagnosis.

cards.front: What are the complications of ERCP for CBD stones?
cards.back:
Retained stones, ERCP-induced pancreatitis (1-2%), pancreatic or biliary sepsis.

ERCP allows sphincterotomy and stone removal from the CBD. Despite its therapeutic utility, ERCP carries procedural risks. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the most common complication. Elective cholecystectomy after successful ERCP is recommended in 25% of patients.

cards.front: What is Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad in acute cholangitis?
cards.back:
Charcot's triad: fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice. Reynolds' pentad: Charcot's triad + hypotension + altered mental status (indicates suppurative/severe cholangitis).

Acute cholangitis results from obstruction of the CBD (most commonly by choledocholithiasis, 60%), leading to biliary stasis and bacterial overgrowth. The most common organisms are E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and anaerobes (mnemonic KEEPS).

cards.front: What is the initial management of acute cholangitis?
cards.back:
NPO, fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, ± NG tube, IV antibiotics (treats 80%). Followed by biliary decompression: ERCP + sphincterotomy (first-line), PTC with catheter drainage (if ERCP fails), or open/laparoscopic CBD exploration + T-tube placement. After resolution, elective cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence.

Suppurative cholangitis carries a 20-30% mortality rate, requiring urgent intervention. IV antibiotics cover Gram-negative enteric organisms and anaerobes. Biliary decompression is the definitive treatment.

cards.front: What is gallstone ileus and what is Rigler's triad?
cards.back:
Gallstone ileus is mechanical bowel obstruction caused by a large gallstone entering the GI tract through a cholecystoenteric fistula (usually duodenal), impacting near the ileocecal valve. Rigler's triad on plain X-ray: pneumobilia (air in biliary tree), small bowel obstruction, and ectopic gallstone (usually in right iliac fossa).

Despite the name, gallstone ileus is a true mechanical obstruction, not a functional ileus. It is a complication of recurrent cholecystitis causing a fistula between the gallbladder and bowel. Treatment is enterolithotomy; the fistula is typically not repaired at the time of emergency surgery.

cards.front: What is Bouveret's syndrome?
cards.back:
Gastric outlet obstruction caused by a large gallstone passing through a cholecystoduodenal fistula and impacting in the duodenum.

Bouveret's syndrome is a rare form of gallstone ileus where the gallstone obstructs the duodenum (proximal GI tract) rather than the ileocecal valve. It presents with gastric outlet obstruction symptoms (vomiting, epigastric pain).

cards.front: What is the treatment for gallstone ileus?
cards.back:
Fluid resuscitation, NG tube decompression, then surgery: enterolithotomy (removal of impacted stone), inspection of the entire small and large bowel for additional proximal stones. The cholecystoenteric fistula is generally NOT addressed at the time of emergency surgery. Cholecystectomy is generally not performed acutely.

Emergency surgery focuses on relieving the obstruction. The fistula may resolve spontaneously or be addressed electively. Simultaneous fistula repair increases operative risk and is deferred unless the patient is stable and the surgeon experienced.

cards.front: A 35-year-old woman on OCP presents with incidentally found 6 cm heterogeneously enhancing liver lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how should it be managed?
cards.back:
Hepatic adenoma. Stop OCP immediately. Given size >5 cm in a woman, surgical excision is indicated due to risk of HCC transformation and spontaneous rupture/hemorrhage.

Hepatic adenoma is strongly associated with OCP use in women aged 20-50. Lesions >5 cm (or any size in men) require excision. CT shows well-demarcated mass with heterogeneous arterial enhancement, isodense on venous phase without washout.

cards.front: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis has a 4 cm arterially enhancing liver lesion with portal venous washout on triphasic CT and AFP of 800. What is the diagnosis and management?
cards.back:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Given the cirrhosis, surgical resection requires adequate hepatic reserve (relative contraindication). Options: liver transplantation if within Milan criteria (single tumour ≤5 cm), bridging therapy (TACE or RFA) while awaiting transplant. If not transplant-eligible: TACE, RFA, sorafenib.

The arterial enhancement + venous washout pattern on triphasic CT is diagnostic for HCC in a cirrhotic liver. AFP >400 is highly suggestive. Milan criteria determine transplant eligibility. Extrahepatic disease and vascular invasion are absolute contraindications to transplant.

cards.front: A 70-year-old diabetic woman in the ICU develops fever, RUQ pain, and leukocytosis. U/S shows a thickened gallbladder wall with sludge but no stones. What is the diagnosis and management?
cards.back:
Acalculous cholecystitis. Manage with NPO, IV fluids, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, and cholecystectomy. If the patient is unstable for surgery, percutaneous cholecystostomy is the alternative. HIDA scan (non-filling gallbladder) is the most useful confirmatory test if U/S is inconclusive.

Acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients due to gallbladder ischemia and stasis (ICU, DM, immunosuppression are key risk factors). Mortality is high if untreated. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is a temporizing measure for poor surgical candidates.

cards.front: A 60-year-old woman presents with fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, hypotension, and confusion. What is the diagnosis, and what is the next step?
cards.back:
Reynolds' pentad indicating severe (suppurative) acute cholangitis. Immediate management: IV resuscitation, NPO, IV antibiotics (covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes), and urgent biliary decompression via ERCP + sphincterotomy. If ERCP fails: PTC or surgical CBD exploration.

Reynolds' pentad (Charcot's triad + shock + altered mental status) indicates life-threatening suppurative cholangitis with biliary sepsis. Mortality is 20-30%. Urgent biliary decompression is critical. Most common cause is choledocholithiasis (60%).

cards.front: What are protective factors against cholesterol gallstone formation?
cards.back:
Statins, physical activity, vitamin C, polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats, nuts, and coffee.

Statins reduce cholesterol secretion into bile. Physical activity and dietary factors improve gallbladder motility and alter bile composition. These factors are relevant for counseling patients with risk factors for gallstone disease.

cards.front: When should prophylactic cholecystectomy be considered for asymptomatic cholelithiasis?
cards.back:
Consider prophylactic cholecystectomy in: increased malignancy risk (choledochal cysts, Caroli's disease, porcelain/calcified gallbladder), sickle cell disease, pediatric patients, patients undergoing bariatric surgery, and immunosuppressed patients.

Most asymptomatic gallstones (80%) do not require treatment; only 18% progress to symptomatic disease within 20 years. Prophylactic cholecystectomy is reserved for high-risk groups where complications or malignant transformation are more likely.

cards.front: What is the timing preference for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in acute cholecystitis?
cards.back:
Early cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) is preferred over delayed (after 6 weeks). Early and delayed have equal morbidity and mortality, but early results in shorter hospitalization and recovery time. Emergent OR is indicated for high-risk presentations (e.g., sepsis).

Canadian guidelines align with international evidence that early cholecystectomy is the standard of care for acute cholecystitis. Delaying surgery does not reduce complications and increases readmission risk. ERCP should be performed prior to surgery if CBD stones are present.

cards.front: What is percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) and when is it used?
cards.back:
PTC is a percutaneous approach to the proximal (intrahepatic) biliary system via hepatic parenchyma. Used for: proximal bile duct obstruction, when ERCP fails or is unavailable. Contraindications: ascites, peri/intrahepatic sepsis, right lower lung/pleural disease. Complications: bile peritonitis, chylothorax, pneumothorax, biliary sepsis, hemobilia.

PTC complements ERCP for biliary access when distal obstruction cannot be crossed endoscopically. It provides access to the intrahepatic biliary system, which ERCP cannot reach in cases of proximal obstruction (e.g., hilar cholangiocarcinoma).

cards.front: A 65-year-old man has a postoperative fever on day 5 after colon surgery. Using the timing of postoperative fever, what is the most likely cause?
cards.back:
POD #3-7 fever is likely infectious: UTI, surgical site infection, IV line infection, septic thrombophlebitis, or leakage at bowel anastomosis (presents with tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, abdominal pain).

Postoperative fever timing helps identify cause: POD 1-2 is usually inflammatory/atelectasis; POD 3-7 is likely infectious; POD 8+ consider abscess, DVT/PE, drug fever, or C. difficile. Anastomotic leak is a critical diagnosis requiring urgent intervention.

cards.front: What is the Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad, and what condition do they describe?
cards.back:
Charcot's triad: fever, RUQ pain, jaundice - describes acute cholangitis. Reynolds' pentad: Charcot's triad + hypotension + altered mental status - indicates suppurative (toxic) cholangitis.

Acute cholangitis results from CBD obstruction leading to biliary stasis and bacterial overgrowth. The most common cause is choledocholithiasis (60%). Common organisms: KEEPS (Klebsiella, Enterococcus, E. coli/Enterobacter, Proteus, Serratia). Emergency biliary decompression via ERCP is required.

cards.front: What is the Rigler's triad and what diagnosis does it suggest?
cards.back:
Rigler's triad: pneumobilia (air in biliary tree), small bowel obstruction, and gallstone (usually in right iliac fossa). It suggests gallstone ileus.

Gallstone ileus occurs when repeated inflammation creates a cholecystoenteric fistula (usually duodenal), allowing a large gallstone to enter the GI tract and impact near the ileocecal valve, causing mechanical bowel obstruction. Treatment is surgical enterolithotomy.

cards.front: A 58-year-old woman presents with a new breast lump. Mammography shows a spiculated mass with microcalcifications. What is the most common type of invasive breast cancer and what are the key prognostic receptor markers?
cards.back:
Invasive ductal carcinoma (80% of invasive breast cancers). Key prognostic markers: estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2/neu status.

Invasive ductal carcinoma presents as a hard, scirrhous mass with infiltrating tentacles. ER/PR positive tumors respond to hormonal therapy (tamoxifen). HER2 positive tumors respond to trastuzumab. Triple-negative (ER-/PR-/HER2-) has the worst prognosis.

cards.front: What BMI criteria are used for bariatric surgery candidacy, and what is the most common and effective procedure?
cards.back:
BMI >=35 without illness OR BMI >30 with 1+ serious comorbidity (DM, CAD, OSA, GERD, severe joint disease). Most common and effective: laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (restrictive + malabsorptive).

Roux-en-Y creates a small gastric pouch (restrictive) anastomosed with a Roux limb of small bowel (malabsorptive). Complications include dumping syndrome, marginal ulcers, cholelithiasis, and metabolic perturbations. Sleeve gastrectomy is an alternative restrictive option.

cards.front: How do you differentiate small bowel obstruction (SBO) from large bowel obstruction (LBO) on clinical presentation and abdominal X-ray?
cards.back:
SBO: early bilious vomiting, colicky pain, less distention (proximal) or moderate (distal), ladder pattern on AXR with dilated loops >3 cm and no colonic gas. LBO: late feculent vomiting, more distention, picture frame appearance on AXR with proximal distention and distal decompression.

SBO is most commonly caused by adhesions (prior surgery), hernias, and tumors. LBO is most commonly caused by colorectal cancer, volvulus, and diverticular disease. Paralytic ileus shows air throughout small bowel and colon with absent bowel sounds.

cards.front: A chronic anal fissure fails to respond to conservative management. What are the pharmacological and surgical treatment options?
cards.back:
Pharmacological: topical nitroglycerin or calcium channel blocker (nifedipine/diltiazem) to increase local blood flow and relieve sphincter spasm. Surgical: lateral internal anal sphincterotomy (most effective, reserved for medically-refractory cases, 5% risk of fecal incontinence). Alternative: botulinum toxin A injection.

Chronic anal fissures present with the triad of fissure, sentinel skin tags, and hypertrophied papillae. 90% are posterior midline due to poor perfusion. The cycle of pain-sphincter spasm-ischemia-poor healing perpetuates chronicity.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.back:
Atelectasis, comprising 90% of postoperative pulmonary complications.

Atelectasis is the most frequent pulmonary complication after surgery. Risk factors include COPD, smoking, obesity, elderly age, and upper abdominal/thoracic surgery. It typically presents as low-grade fever on POD #1.

cards.front: A patient develops fever on POD #5-8. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.back:
Surgical site infection (SSI). Typical SSI presents with fever POD #5-8, localized pain, erythema, induration, purulent discharge, and warmth.

SSIs typically manifest POD #5-8, although Streptococcus and Clostridium can present within 24 hours. The wound should be inspected, compressed, and swabbed for culture. Treatment involves reopening the wound and healing by secondary intention.

cards.front: What are the four classifications of surgical wound contamination and their approximate infection rates?
cards.back:
Clean (2%), Clean-contaminated (3-4%), Contaminated (10%), Dirty/Infected (30-40%).

Clean wounds have no entry into hollow viscus. Clean-contaminated involves controlled entry into hollow viscus without spillage (e.g., routine cholecystectomy). Contaminated involves major wound contamination (e.g., bowel spillage). Dirty indicates established infection present before surgery.

cards.front: What is the most important initial sign of wound dehiscence?
cards.back:
Serosanguinous (salmon-coloured) drainage from the wound, typically on POD #1-3 or #7-10.

Wound dehiscence is disruption of a primarily closed wound. The most common presentation is serosanguinous drainage. Evisceration (burst abdomen) is a surgical emergency requiring operative re-closure. A normal healing wound should have a palpable 'healing ridge.'

cards.front: What is the preferred preoperative antibiotic regimen for most surgeries?
cards.back:
Cefazolin + metronidazole (or if beta-lactam allergy: clindamycin + gentamicin or vancomycin), given within 1 hour pre-incision.

Prophylactic antibiotics should be administered within 1 hour of incision and re-dosed every 1-2 half-lives in the OR. They are not required for low-risk clean surgery such as elective thyroidectomy or cholecystectomy. Postoperative antibiotics should be reserved for suspected or documented infection.

cards.front: A rapidly expanding neck hematoma after thyroid surgery compromises the airway. What is the most important immediate management?
cards.back:
Protect the airway with intubation. Consider opening the wound emergently at bedside. A suture kit should be at bedside for all neck surgery patients.

Neck hematomas are more clinically relevant in small working spaces like thyroid or breast surgery due to risk of airway edema and compression. A rapidly expanding neck hematoma is a surgical emergency where airway protection takes priority.

cards.front: What are the systemic risk factors for wound dehiscence?
cards.back:
Male sex, smoking, malnutrition (hypoalbuminemia, vitamin C deficiency), connective tissue diseases, immunosuppression, pulmonary disease, ascites, steroids, chemotherapy, obesity, age, sepsis, and uremia. DM alone is NOT a risk factor.

Both local and systemic factors contribute to wound dehiscence. Notably, diabetes mellitus alone is not a risk factor. The small bites suture technique is superior to large bites for preventing incisional hernia in midline incisions.

cards.front: What is the timeline for return of GI motility after abdominal surgery?
cards.back:
Gastric and small bowel motility returns by 24-48 hours; colonic motility returns by 3-5 days.

Paralytic ileus is a temporary, reversible impairment of intestinal motility most frequently caused by abdominal operations. If ileus persists beyond expected timeframes, investigate for electrolyte abnormalities, medications (especially opiates), and intra-abdominal pathology with CT.

cards.front: What is the hallmark clinical feature of early intestinal ischemia?
cards.back:
Pain 'out of keeping' (out of proportion) to physical findings.

In acute mesenteric ischemia, patients present with severe abdominal pain but relatively benign physical exam findings early in the course. CT angiography is the gold standard for acute arterial ischemia. An acute abdomen with metabolic acidosis should raise suspicion for mesenteric ischemia.

cards.front: What are the top 3 causes of small bowel obstruction (SBO) in order?
cards.back:
Adhesions (75%), Bulge (hernias), Cancer (neoplasms) — mnemonic ABC.

Prior abdominal surgery causing adhesions is by far the most common cause. SBO presents with colicky periumbilical pain, N/V, obstipation, and abdominal distention. Inability to pass flatus is the most useful clinical indicator.

cards.front: When is immediate surgery indicated in small bowel obstruction?
cards.back:
When there are signs of ischemia, necrosis, or perforation: fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, worsening pain, metabolic/lactic acidosis, and tachypnea. Radiologic signs include free air, closed-loop obstruction, pneumatosis intestinalis, and portal venous gas.

Most adhesive SBOs can be initially managed conservatively with NG tube decompression and IV fluid resuscitation. However, patients with a 'virgin abdomen' (no prior surgery) presenting with SBO should have surgery ASAP. Closed-loop obstruction also requires immediate exploration.

cards.front: What is the mortality associated with strangulating SBO versus non-strangulating SBO?
cards.back:
Non-strangulating: <1% mortality. Strangulating: 8% (25% if >36 hours). Ischemic: up to 50%.

The prognosis of SBO is related to etiology. Open surgery has a four-fold increase in risk of SBO within 5 years compared to laparoscopic surgery. Surgical intervention is associated with lower risk of recurrence.

cards.front: What are the top 3 causes of large bowel obstruction (LBO)?
cards.back:
Colon cancer (60%), Diverticulitis (10%), Volvulus.

In LBO, a competent ileocecal valve creates a closed-loop obstruction (80-90% of cases), which is dangerous because massive colonic distention leads to cecal wall ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. Impending perforation should be suspected when cecum diameter exceeds 12 cm.

cards.front: What differentiates paralytic ileus from mechanical bowel obstruction on physical examination?
cards.back:
In paralytic ileus, bowel sounds are diminished or absent and pain is diffuse and non-colicky. In mechanical obstruction, bowel sounds are initially hyperactive with colicky pain.

Paralytic ileus involves temporary impairment of intestinal motility without mechanical obstruction. Most common causes are abdominal operations, infections, opiates, and electrolyte abnormalities. Passing gas is the most useful indicator of resolution.

cards.front: A 65-year-old presents with acute onset colicky abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and pain out of proportion to exam findings. What is the most likely diagnosis and gold standard investigation?
cards.back:
Acute mesenteric ischemia. Gold standard investigation is CT angiography.

Acute mesenteric ischemia can be caused by arterial occlusion (thrombotic or embolic), non-occlusive ischemia (from hypoperfusion), or mesenteric venous thrombosis. Common sites include SMA territory and 'watershed' areas of the colon (splenic flexure, left colon, sigmoid).

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of appendicitis and why does the pain migrate?
cards.back:
Pain initially periumbilical (visceral, poorly localized), then localizes to McBurney's point (RLQ). The migration occurs because disease progresses from visceral irritation (referred midgut pain) to parietal peritoneal irritation.

The most reliable feature of appendicitis is progression of signs and symptoms. Classic order is abdominal pain, then anorexia, then N/V. McBurney's point is located 1/3 the distance from ASIS to umbilicus on the right side.

cards.front: What are the three signs of appendicitis and what anatomical positions do they correspond to?
cards.back:
McBurney's sign (inferior appendix): RLQ tenderness. Psoas sign (retrocecal appendix): pain on hip flexion against resistance. Obturator sign (pelvic appendix): pain on flexion then internal rotation of hip.

Rovsing's sign (palpation of left abdomen causes McBurney's point tenderness) suggests peritoneal irritation. McBurney's sign is present whenever the appendiceal base is under McBurney's point, regardless of appendix tip position.

cards.front: What is the optimal imaging for diagnosing appendicitis, and what is the role of antibiotics-only treatment?
cards.back:
CT scan (94-100% accuracy) is optimal. US has 90-94% accuracy but cannot rule out appendicitis. Antibiotics alone have 80-90% success rate for non-perforated appendicitis without appendicolith, but 40-49% undergo appendectomy by 3-4 years.

Appendectomy remains the gold standard treatment. For perforated appendicitis with abscess, consider radiologic drainage and antibiotics with interval appendectomy. MRI may be used in pregnancy if ultrasound is non-diagnostic.

cards.front: What is the frequency and anatomical classification of abdominal hernias?
cards.back:
50% indirect inguinal, 25% direct inguinal, 8-10% incisional, 5% femoral, 3-8% umbilical. Lifetime risk: males 20-25%, females 2%.

Indirect inguinal hernias are the most common hernia in both men and women. They pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. Direct inguinal hernias pass through Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery.

cards.front: What are the borders of Hesselbach's triangle and what hernia passes through it?
cards.back:
Lateral: inferior epigastric artery. Inferior: inguinal ligament. Medial: lateral margin of rectus sheath. Direct inguinal hernias pass through Hesselbach's triangle.

Direct inguinal hernias are medial to the inferior epigastric artery (mnemonic: MD = Medial = Direct). Indirect inguinal hernias are lateral to the inferior epigastric artery (LI = Lateral = Indirect). This distinction is important for surgical planning.

cards.front: Which type of hernia has the highest risk of strangulation?
cards.back:
Femoral > indirect inguinal > direct inguinal. Small, new hernias are more likely to strangulate.

Strangulation is a surgical emergency where the vascular supply of protruded viscus is compromised. Do NOT attempt manual reduction if septic or if hernial sac contents are gangrenous, as this will introduce gangrenous contents intraperitoneally.

cards.front: What is a Richter's hernia and why is it dangerous?
cards.back:
Only part of the bowel circumference (usually antimesenteric border) is incarcerated, so the bowel may not be obstructed. A strangulated Richter's hernia may self-reduce and be overlooked, leaving a gangrenous segment at risk of perforation.

Richter's hernia is dangerous because the absence of obstructive symptoms can lead to delayed diagnosis. Other special hernia types include Littre's (Meckel's diverticulum), Amyand's (appendix), and sliding hernia (retroperitoneal structure forms wall of sac).

cards.front: What distinguishes indirect from direct inguinal hernia based on anatomy and etiology?
cards.back:
Indirect: congenital (patent processus vaginalis), lateral to inferior epigastric artery, originates at deep inguinal ring, often descends into scrotum. Direct: acquired (transversalis fascia weakness), medial to inferior epigastric artery, through Hesselbach's triangle, usually does not descend into scrotum.

Indirect inguinal hernias are 5x more common than direct and have <1% recurrence rate versus 3-4% for direct. Indirect hernias are 5-10x more common in males than females and have 5% lifetime incidence in males.

cards.front: What is the Hinchey classification for diverticulitis and how does it guide treatment?
cards.back:
Stage 1: Phlegmon/small pericolic abscess (medical). Stage 2: Large abscess/fistula (drainage + resection). Stage 3: Purulent peritonitis (resection or Hartmann). Stage 4: Feculent peritonitis (Hartmann procedure).

Mortality rates are 6% for purulent peritonitis and 35% for feculent peritonitis. For uncomplicated diverticulitis, antibiotics are no longer routinely recommended. Surgery is indicated for Hinchey 3-4 and for patients who are unstable with peritonitis.

cards.front: What is the most common fistula complication of diverticulitis?
cards.back:
Colovesical fistula (most common). Others include coloenteric, colovaginal, and colocutaneous fistulas.

Complications of diverticulitis occur in 25% of cases and include abscess, fistula, colonic obstruction from strictures, and perforation. CT scan is the test of choice with 97% sensitivity and 99% specificity. Colonoscopy should be done after resolution of acute episode.

cards.front: What defines a Hartmann procedure and what are its indications?
cards.back:
Colon resection + end colostomy with closure of rectal stump. Used for unstable patients with peritonitis, Hinchey stage 3-4 diverticulitis, and emergent situations where primary anastomosis is unsafe. Colostomy reversal in 3-6 months.

For more stable patients with Hinchey 3-4, colonic resection with primary anastomosis plus diverting loop ileostomy is becoming more common with benefits for mortality and morbidity compared to the traditional Hartmann procedure.

cards.front: What is the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colorectal cancer?
cards.back:
Adenomatous polyps are premalignant lesions that progress through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. Malignant potential is: villous > tubulovillous > tubular. Risk increases with size >1 cm, villous histology, and multiple polyps.

Colorectal carcinomas rarely arise de novo. 30% of the population have polyps by age 50. Villous polyps are large (>2 cm), sessile, and have higher malignant potential. Tubular polyps are smaller (<2 cm), pedunculated, with lower malignant potential.

cards.front: What are the Amsterdam Criteria for diagnosing Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)?
cards.back:
The '3-2-1 rule': 3+ relatives with Lynch-associated cancers (1 must be 1st-degree relative of other 2), 2+ generations involved, 1 case diagnosed before age 50, and FAP excluded.

Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited CRC susceptibility syndrome (3% of CRC). It is autosomal dominant with mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, PMS2). Lifetime CRC risk is 70-80%. Treatment is total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis.

cards.front: An elderly patient presents with iron-deficiency anemia. What malignancy must be investigated?
cards.back:
Colon cancer (especially right-sided). Right colon cancers present with weight loss, weakness, dark blood mixed in stool, and iron-deficiency anemia.

Right-sided colon cancers are often insidious, presenting with anemia and RLQ mass rather than obstruction. Left-sided cancers present with constipation, altered bowel habits, decreased stool calibre, and rectal bleeding. Rectal cancers cause obstruction, tenesmus, and rectal bleeding.

cards.front: What is Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) and when should surgery be performed?
cards.back:
Autosomal dominant APC gene mutation causing hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas usually by age 20, with virtually 100% lifetime risk of colon cancer. Surgery indicated by ages 17-20.

FAP accounts for <1% of colorectal cancers. Surgical options include total proctocolectomy with ileostomy or restorative proctocolectomy with ileal-pouch anal anastomosis. Variants include Gardner's syndrome (FAP + osteomas, desmoids) and Turcot syndrome (FAP + CNS tumours).

cards.front: What are the internal hemorrhoid grades and their treatment?
cards.back:
1st degree: bleeds, no prolapse → conservative + rubber band ligation. 2nd degree: prolapse with straining, spontaneous reduction → rubber band ligation. 3rd degree: prolapse requiring manual reduction → rubber band ligation or hemorrhoidectomy. 4th degree: permanently prolapsed → hemorrhoidectomy.

Internal hemorrhoids arise from superior hemorrhoidal veins above the dentate line (portal circulation), usually at 3, 7, 11 o'clock positions in lithotomy. They cause painless bright red rectal bleeding. Always rule out colon cancer in patients >50 with rectal bleeding.

cards.front: What is the most effective treatment for chronic anal fissure refractory to medical management?
cards.back:
Lateral internal anal sphincterotomy (most effective treatment). It relieves sphincter spasm to increase blood flow and promote healing, but has a 5% chance of fecal incontinence.

Chronic anal fissures present with the triad of fissure, sentinel skin tags, and hypertrophied papillae. 90% are posterior midline due to poor perfusion. Medical treatment includes topical nitroglycerin or calcium channel blockers. Botulinum toxin is an alternative.

cards.front: What is Goodsall's rule for anal fistulas?
cards.back:
Fistulas with external openings anterior to a transverse line through the anus have a straight course and exit anteriorly. Those with posterior external openings have a curved tract and originate in the posterior midline.

Anorectal fistulas develop in 50% of patients after I&D of perianal abscess. Treatment depends on the fistula's relationship to the sphincter: low fistulas are treated with fistulotomy, while high fistulas (involving external sphincter) require staged fistulotomy with seton placement.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis and what investigation strongly suggests gallstone etiology?
cards.back:
Gallstones (45% of acute pancreatitis). ALT >150 U/L strongly suggests gallstone etiology.

Gallstone pancreatitis occurs from pancreatic duct obstruction causing autodigestion. The stone passes spontaneously in ~90% of cases. Cholecystectomy should be performed during the same admission as there is 25-60% recurrence if surgery is not done.

cards.front: What are Ranson's criteria for acute pancreatitis severity?
cards.back:
At admission: Age >55, WBC >16, Glucose >11 mmol/L, LDH >350, AST >250. At 48h: Hct drop >10%, BUN rise >1.8 mmol/L, Ca <2 mmol/L, base deficit >4 mmol/L, fluid sequestration >6L, PaO2 <60 mmHg. Score ≥3 = severe pancreatitis.

Ranson's criteria help determine prognosis. A score <3 means severe pancreatitis is unlikely (2% mortality). A score of 3-5 indicates 15% mortality, and >5 indicates 40% mortality. APACHE II score is also used for severe acute pancreatitis prognosis.

cards.front: When is ERCP urgently indicated in gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.back:
When there is an impacted CBD stone or concomitant cholangitis.

Most gallstones pass spontaneously (~90%). Cholecystectomy during the same admission is recommended to prevent recurrence. Antibiotics are not indicated for initial diagnosis of pancreatitis unless there are clear signs of infection on imaging.

cards.front: What is the Puestow procedure and when is it indicated?
cards.back:
Lateral pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow procedure) is a drainage procedure for chronic pancreatitis when the ductal system is dilated. It improves pain in 80% of patients.

Surgical options for chronic pancreatitis depend on anatomy: drainage (Puestow) if dilated duct, Whipple for proximal disease, distal pancreatectomy for distal disease, and total pancreatectomy for refractory disease. The hallmark of chronic pancreatitis is recurrent abdominal pain.

cards.front: What is the presentation of pancreatic cancer and the most useful serum marker?
cards.back:
Most common symptoms: abdominal pain, jaundice, and weight loss. CA 19-9 is the most useful serum marker. Vague abdominal pain with weight loss in a patient >50 is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise.

Head tumours (70%) present with jaundice, steatorrhea, and weight loss with Courvoisier's sign. Body/tail tumours (30%) present later and are usually unresectable (80%). Only 10-20% of pancreatic cancers are resectable. Overall 5-year survival is only 1%.

cards.front: What is the Whipple procedure and what are its indications?
cards.back:
Pancreaticoduodenectomy: resection of pancreatic head, duodenum, distal CBD, gallbladder, and distal stomach. Reconstruction involves pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy. Indicated for resectable pancreatic head cancer (<5% mortality).

Resectability requires no involvement of liver, peritoneum, or major vasculature (hepatic artery, SMA, SMV, portal vein, IVC, aorta) and no distant metastasis. Adjuvant chemotherapy (gemcitabine + capecitabine) is recommended. 5-year survival after resection is 20%.

cards.front: What is the most common intra-abdominal organ injured in blunt trauma?
cards.back:
The spleen. It can also occur in people with splenomegaly. Kehr's sign (left shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation) may be present.

FAST ultrasound is used for hemodynamically unstable trauma patients. CT with contrast is used once stable. Treatment ranges from non-operative (bed rest, serial hematocrit, splenic artery embolization) to operative (splenorrhaphy or splenectomy for unstable patients).

cards.front: What vaccinations are required after splenectomy and what is the most feared complication?
cards.back:
Pneumococcal, H. influenzae, and meningococcal vaccines (ideally 2 weeks pre- or postoperative). The most feared complication is overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis from encapsulated organisms (4% of splenectomized patients).

Post-splenectomy sepsis risk is highest in patients <16 years. Liberal use of penicillin is recommended especially in children <6 years. Other complications include postoperative thrombocytosis, portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, and increased risk of malignancy and DVT/PE.

cards.front: What is the triple test for diagnosis of a breast mass?
cards.back:
1) Clinical breast exam, 2) Imaging (mammography + US if ≥30; US alone if <30 or pregnant/lactating), 3) Pathology (core needle biopsy is most common).

US-guided core needle biopsy is preferred over FNA or excisional biopsy for diagnosis. If all three components of the triple test are concordant and benign, the negative predictive value approaches 100%. Excisional biopsy should not be done for initial diagnosis if possible.

cards.front: What are the key differences between DCIS and LCIS?
cards.back:
DCIS: proliferation within ducts, detected as mammographic microcalcifications, 35% risk of invasive cancer in same breast in 10 years, treated with excision + radiation. LCIS: contained within lobules, no mammographic findings, ~1%/year risk of invasive carcinoma in either breast, managed with surveillance.

DCIS is treated surgically (lumpectomy + radiation or mastectomy for large/multifocal disease). LCIS is considered a risk factor rather than a precursor lesion. LCIS is often multicentric and bilateral, so wide excision is not needed. Both may benefit from tamoxifen.

cards.front: When is breast conservation surgery (BCS) contraindicated?
cards.back:
Absolute contraindications: inflammatory breast cancer, extensive malignant calcifications/multifocal tumours, failure to obtain tumour-free margins after re-excision, and inability to receive radiation (pregnancy, prior radiation, collagen vascular disease).

BCS plus radiation has equivalent survival to mastectomy for stage I-II disease. BCS can be offered to most women with stage I-II disease. There is no survival benefit of mastectomy over BCS plus radiation when local control is achieved.

cards.front: What is a sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) and when is axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) required?
cards.back:
SLNB uses technetium-99 + blue dye to identify the first draining lymph node. Proceed to ALND if >3 positive sentinel nodes. With 1-3 positive nodes, whole breast radiation may be an alternative to ALND.

SLNB is performed in clinically node-negative invasive breast cancer. It has a 5% false-negative rate. ALND carries risk of arm lymphedema (10-15%), especially with concurrent radiation. Studies show no survival benefit of ALND over SLNB alone in patients with 1-2 positive sentinel nodes.

cards.front: What is the most common type of invasive breast cancer and what is the most aggressive form?
cards.back:
Invasive ductal carcinoma is most common (80%). Inflammatory carcinoma (1-3%) is the most aggressive form — it invades dermal lymphatics causing erythema, peau d'orange, and swollen breast.

Invasive lobular carcinoma (8-10%) is harder to detect on mammography due to lack of microcalcifications. Paget's disease of the breast involves nipple invasion with scaling and ulceration. Peau d'orange in inflammatory carcinoma automatically stages the cancer as IIIb-IV.

cards.front: What are the complications of thyroidectomy?
cards.back:
Lobectomy: recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy (hoarseness), neck hematoma. Total thyroidectomy: same plus hypoparathyroidism/hypocalcemia, bilateral RLN palsy (may require tracheostomy). 20-75% need thyroxine after lobectomy; 100% after total thyroidectomy.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove and is at risk during thyroid surgery. Bilateral RLN palsy can cause airway obstruction requiring tracheostomy. Hypocalcemia from inadvertent parathyroid removal is treated with calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

cards.front: What is Whipple's triad and what does it diagnose?
cards.back:
Whipple's triad: 1) Symptomatic fasting hypoglycemia, 2) Serum glucose <2.8 mmol/L, 3) Relief of symptoms when glucose is administered. It diagnoses insulinoma.

Insulinoma is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm (10% associated with MEN1). Lab findings include decreased serum glucose with increased insulin and C-peptide. Only 10% are malignant. Treatment is enucleation for solitary insulinomas.

cards.front: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and where are most gastrinomas located?
cards.back:
Gastrin-secreting tumour causing severe PUD, multiple ulcers in atypical locations, and severe esophagitis. 70-90% found in Passaro's triangle (head of pancreas, 2nd portion of duodenum, cystic duct-CBD confluence). 50% are malignant.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is associated with MEN1. Serum gastrin levels are usually >1000 pg/mL. 90% develop peptic ulcers. Treatment includes surgical resection, high-dose PPI, and octreotide for non-surgical candidates.

cards.front: What are the indications for surgery in peptic ulcer disease?
cards.back:
Hemorrhage (most common emergency indication), perforation, gastric outlet obstruction, refractory to medical management (8-12 weeks), and suspicion of malignancy.

Surgery for PUD is increasingly rare due to H. pylori eradication and PPI therapy. For perforated duodenal ulcer, omental (Graham) patch is the most common treatment. Posterior duodenal ulcers tend to bleed (gastroduodenal artery), while anterior ulcers tend to perforate.

cards.front: What is the hallmark presentation of perforated duodenal ulcer on CXR?
cards.back:
Free air under the diaphragm (seen in 70% of patients). Clinical features include sudden onset of pain (may track to RLQ via right paracolic gutter), acute abdomen with rigid diffuse guarding, and ileus.

Initial chemical peritonitis is followed by bacterial peritonitis. Treatment is oversewing the ulcer (plication) with omental Graham patch. This is the most common treatment for perforated duodenal ulcer. H. pylori eradication should follow postoperatively.

cards.front: What is dumping syndrome and how does early differ from late?
cards.back:
Early (15-30 min): rapid emptying of hyperosmotic chyme → jejunal distention → cramping, bloating, emesis, vasomotor symptoms (dizziness, tachycardia, diaphoresis). Late (3 h): hypoglycemia from postprandial insulin peak.

Early dumping is treated with frequent small meals high in fibre/protein, low in carbohydrates, and avoiding liquids with meals. Late dumping is treated with a small snack 2 hours after meals. Dumping syndrome is a complication of gastric surgery and usually resolves within 1 year.

cards.front: What is the most common benign liver tumour and how should it be managed?
cards.back:
Cavernous hemangioma. Avoid biopsy (risk of hemorrhage). No treatment if asymptomatic. Surgical resection for symptomatic patients or those with large hemangiomas causing mass effect.

On CT, hemangiomas show peripheral enhancement on arterial phase with centripetal filling on delayed phases. On US, they appear as homogeneous hyperechoic masses. Those >10 cm are considered 'giant' and may cause consumptive coagulopathy in children.

cards.front: What are the criteria for tension pneumothorax and its immediate management?
cards.back:
Contralateral tracheal deviation, hypotension/shock, diminished breath sounds, hyperresonance on the affected side. Immediate management: needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and a life-threatening emergency. Air enters the pleural space via a one-way valve mechanism, raising intrapleural pressure and causing cardiovascular collapse. Do not delay treatment for imaging.

cards.front: What is the management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.back:
Stable, small (<3 cm), minimal symptoms: observation + O2. Symptomatic or large (>3 cm): aspiration or chest tube. Unstable/tension: needle decompression then chest tube, VATS bullectomy if unsuccessful (25-50% failure rate).

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without underlying lung disease, typically from rupture of apical subpleural blebs. Risk factors include smoking, male sex, family history, and Marfan's syndrome. Secondary pneumothorax occurs with underlying lung disease and generally requires more aggressive management.

cards.front: What is the mnemonic for the differential of anterior mediastinal masses?
cards.back:
The 4 Ts: Thymoma, Thyroid (goitre), Teratoma, Tumours (lymphoma, parathyroid, angiomatous).

Anterior mediastinal masses are more likely malignant. 50% are asymptomatic (mainly benign); when symptomatic, 50% are malignant. If AFP, β-hCG, or LDH are elevated, no biopsy is needed as these are pathognomonic for germ cell tumour.

cards.front: What is the most common primary lung cancer subtype in nonsmokers and what is the screening recommendation?
cards.back:
Adenocarcinoma (most common in nonsmokers, peripheral location). Screening: annual low-dose CT for high-risk patients aged 55-74 with ≥30 pack-year history who are current smokers or quit within 15 years.

Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer mortality worldwide. NSCLC (85-90%) includes adenocarcinoma, SCC, and large cell. SCLC (10-15%) is central, strongly associated with smoking, and usually disseminated at presentation. FEV1 and DLCO must be ≥40% predicted to tolerate surgical resection.

cards.front: What paraneoplastic syndromes are associated with small cell lung cancer?
cards.back:
Cushing's syndrome (ectopic ACTH), SIADH, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. SCLC is the most common lung cancer type associated with paraneoplastic syndromes.

SCC is associated with hypercalcemia (PTHrP). Other paraneoplastic syndromes include HPOA/clubbing (NSCLC), Trousseau's syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis in NSCLC), and carcinoid syndrome (bronchial carcinoid). These syndromes may precede the diagnosis of lung cancer.

cards.front: What is the management of esophageal perforation (Boerhaave's syndrome)?
cards.back:
If contained and stable (Cameron's criteria): NPO, antibiotics, IV fluids, percutaneous drainage. If deteriorating or toxic: surgical repair. <24h: primary closure with muscle flap. >24h or non-viable esophagus: diversion and exclusion with delayed reconstruction.

Boerhaave's syndrome is transmural esophageal perforation from forceful vomiting (versus Mallory-Weiss tear which is partial thickness). Diagnosis: CXR shows pneumomediastinum, Gastrografin swallow study first, then dilute barium. Mortality is 10-50% depending on timing.

cards.front: What are the types of hiatus hernia and which is most common?
cards.back:
Type I (sliding, 90%): GE junction herniates above diaphragm. Type II (paraesophageal, <10%): fundus herniates with GE junction in normal position. Type III (mixed): most common indication for surgical repair, combination of I and II. Type IV: other organs herniate (colon, spleen).

Sliding hernias are managed with lifestyle modifications and PPI. Paraesophageal and mixed hernias require surgical repair due to risk of incarceration, strangulation (gastric volvulus), and hemorrhage. Nissen fundoplication (360° wrap) is the most commonly performed anti-reflux procedure.

cards.front: What is achalasia and what is the classic barium esophagram finding?
cards.back:
Esophageal smooth muscle motility disorder where the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax. Classic finding: smooth tapering of the lower esophagus to a 'bird's beak' appearance on barium esophagram.

Esophageal manometry shows incomplete LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. Treatment options include pharmacologic (nitrates, CCBs), endoscopic botulinum toxin injection, pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, and peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).

cards.front: What is the diagnostic criteria and management for Ogilvie's syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction)?
cards.back:
Distention of colon without mechanical obstruction. CT shows cecal dilatation (≥12 cm = increased perforation risk). Treatment: if cecum <12 cm: treat underlying cause, NPO, NG tube. If cecum ≥12 cm: colonoscopic decompression or neostigmine.

Ogilvie's syndrome is most commonly associated with trauma, infection, and cardiac disease (MI, CHF). It is caused by autonomic motor dysregulation. Most cases resolve with conservative management. Surgery (extremely rare) is reserved for perforation, ischemia, or failure of conservative management.

cards.front: What are the diagnostic criteria for toxic megacolon?
cards.back:
Radiologic evidence of dilated colon >6 cm PLUS 3 of: fever, HR >120, WBC >10.5, anemia PLUS 1 of: dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, hypotension, or altered LOC.

Toxic megacolon is caused by IBD (UC > Crohn's) or infectious colitis (C. difficile, Salmonella). Sudden improvement of diarrhea may signify onset of megacolon. Triggers include hypokalemia, opioids, and anticholinergics. Treatment includes NPO, antibiotics, and surgery if no improvement in 48-72 hours. Mortality is 25-30%.

cards.front: What is the classic radiographic sign of sigmoid volvulus?
cards.back:
The 'coffee bean' sign on AXR with the central cleft pointing to the LLQ. Barium enema shows 'ace of spades' or 'bird's beak' appearance.

Sigmoid volvulus accounts for 65% of all volvulus cases. It is most common in elderly patients >70 years. Initial treatment is endoscopic decompression with rigid/flexible sigmoidoscopy and rectal tube. Elective surgery is recommended due to 50-70% recurrence. For cecal volvulus, the central cleft points to RLQ.

cards.front: What is the surgical management of ulcerative colitis and what is the operation of choice?
cards.back:
Restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) + rectal mucosectomy is the operation of choice. In emergency: total colectomy + ileostomy with Hartmann closure of rectum.

Indications for surgery in UC include failure of medical management, hemorrhage, perforation, toxic megacolon, fulminant colitis, and cancer risk reduction (1-2%/year after 10 years of disease). Total proctocolectomy eliminates cancer risk. Perforation is the leading cause of death from UC.

cards.front: How does Crohn's disease surgical management differ from ulcerative colitis?
cards.back:
Crohn's surgery is NOT curative (only symptomatic relief). ~70% of patients require surgery. Resection margins only need to be free of gross disease (microscopic disease is irrelevant). Stricturoplasty is used to avoid excessive bowel resection.

The most common surgical indication in Crohn's is SBO due to stricture (50% of cases). Stricturoplasty widens the lumen in scarred bowel without resection. It is contraindicated in acute inflammation. 10-year recurrence rates are 25-50% for ileocolic disease.

cards.front: What is the most common postoperative day for PE and what is the prophylaxis?
cards.back:
Most commonly POD #8-10, but can occur anytime postoperatively. Prophylaxis: subcutaneous heparin or LMWH, compression stockings, and sequential compression devices.

PE presents with sudden onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and unilateral leg swelling/pain (DVT source). Diagnosis is by CT chest. Treatment is IV heparin or LMWH bridging to therapeutic anticoagulation for minimum 3-6 months. Greenfield (IVC) filter if anticoagulation is contraindicated.

cards.front: When does postoperative MI most commonly occur and how does it present?
cards.back:
Most commonly on day of operation or POD #3-4 (when third-space fluid shifts back to intravascular compartment). Often SILENT without chest pain — may present only with new-onset CHF, arrhythmias, or hypotension.

Risk is highest in patients with MI within 6 months (but risk never returns to baseline). Incidence is 0.5% in previously asymptomatic men >50, with a 40-fold increase in those with previous MI. Intraoperative hypotension and operations >3 hours increase risk.

cards.front: What is the timing and presentation of intra-abdominal abscess after surgery?
cards.back:
Manifests at least 5-7 days after surgery (takes time to form collection). Presents with persistent spiking fever, dull pain, weight loss, and leukocytosis. Common sites include pelvis, Morrison's pouch, subphrenic space, and paracolic gutters.

Diagnosis is by CT with IV and water-soluble contrast. Treatment is drain placement by interventional radiology (preferred), laparoscopy, or open drainage, followed by antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin-tazobactam).

cards.front: What are the indications for bariatric surgery?
cards.back:
BMI ≥35 without comorbidities OR BMI ≥30 with 1+ serious comorbidity (DM, CAD, sleep apnea, GERD, severe joint disease). For Asian patients: lower BMI threshold by 2.5 due to higher prevalence of truncal obesity.

Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is the most common and most effective procedure but has higher complication rates. Sleeve gastrectomy is a restrictive procedure. Complications include anastomotic leak (tachycardia may be the only sign in morbidly obese patients), dumping syndrome, and nutritional deficiencies.

cards.front: What are the classic signs of gallbladder carcinoma?
cards.back:
Non-specific RUQ pain, palpable RUQ mass, Courvoisier's sign (enlarged gallbladder + painless jaundice), jaundice (50%), anorexia, weight loss. Most are adenocarcinomas. May be incidental finding on cholecystectomy (~1% open, 0.1% laparoscopic).

Risk factors include chronic symptomatic gallstones (70%), gallbladder polyps, porcelain gallbladder, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Prognosis is poor (20% 5-year survival) due to late detection. If suspected preoperatively, open cholecystectomy should be considered to avoid tumour seeding.

cards.front: What is a Klatskin tumour?
cards.back:
A cholangiocarcinoma located at the bifurcation of the common hepatic duct. Treatment for upper third bile duct lesions is duct resection + Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy ± liver resection.

Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of bile duct epithelial cells. Risk factors include PSC, choledochal cyst, Clonorchis sinensis infection, and chronic intrahepatic stones. LFTs show an obstructive picture. CA 19-9 and CEA may be elevated. Overall 5-year survival is 30% for localized disease.

cards.front: What are the mnemonic signs of metastatic gastric carcinoma?
cards.back:
Virchow's node: left supraclavicular node. Blumer's shelf: mass in pouch of Douglas. Krukenberg tumour: metastases to ovary. Sister Mary Joseph node: umbilical nodule. Irish's node: left axillary nodes.

Gastric carcinoma is the 5th most common cancer worldwide with M:F = 3:2. Risk factors include H. pylori, pernicious anemia, previous partial gastrectomy, salt-preserved foods, smoking, and blood type A. An ulcer that fails to heal or a lesion on the greater curvature should raise suspicion.

cards.front: What is the presentation and management of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in infants?
cards.back:
Presents at 1-8 weeks (most commonly 6-8 weeks) with projectile non-bilious vomiting 30-60 min after feeds. Baby is hungry after vomiting. Palpable 'olive' mass in RUQ. Labs show hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Treatment: correct electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy.

M:F = 4:1. US confirms diagnosis showing pyloric length >17 mm and muscle thickness >4 mm. Paradoxical aciduria occurs because kidneys exchange H+ for K+ to conserve potassium. The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is curative and can be performed open or laparoscopically.

cards.front: What is the mnemonic for why fistulae stay open (FRIENDO)?
cards.back:
Foreign body, Radiation, Infection/IBD, Epithelialization, Neoplasm, Distal obstruction, Other (steroids inhibit closure).

A fistula is an abnormal communication between two epithelialized surfaces. For high-output fistulas, the patient may need to be NPO with long-term TPN. Treatment includes decreasing secretion with octreotide and surgical intervention for non-closing fistulas.

cards.front: What distinguishes carcinoid syndrome from a non-functional carcinoid tumour?
cards.back:
Carcinoid syndrome (<10% of carcinoids) requires liver metastasis so that serotonin/vasoactive peptides bypass hepatic inactivation and enter systemic circulation. Symptoms: flushing, diarrhea, bronchoconstriction, and right-sided heart failure.

Carcinoid tumours originate from enterochromaffin cells. Most are in the appendix (46%) and distal ileum (28%). Diagnosis includes elevated urinary 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite) and serum chromogranin A. Treatment is surgical resection; octreotide for carcinoid syndrome.

cards.front: What is the hallmark presentation of malrotation with midgut volvulus in a neonate?
cards.back:
Bilious emesis in a neonate is midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. The cardinal sign is bilious vomiting, especially with a non-distended abdomen. Requires EMERGENT laparotomy.

Malrotation results from failure of gut rotation around the SMA. The Ladd procedure involves counterclockwise reduction of volvulus, division of Ladd's bands, broadening of the mesentery, and appendectomy. Upper GI series shows the duodenojejunal junction right of midline. Mortality with extensive necrosis is 65%.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of intussusception and its classic presentation?
cards.back:
Most common cause of bowel obstruction in ages 6-36 months. Usually idiopathic, starting at ileocecal junction. Classic triad: episodic colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and 'currant-jelly' stool (mucosal necrosis/sloughing). A sausage-shaped abdominal mass may be palpable.

Non-operative management with air contrast enema is first-line for reduction. Operative reduction is needed if there is failure to reduce, peritonitis, or compromised bowel. There is a 10% recurrence rate. Pathologic lead points (polyps, Meckel's, lymphoma) should be considered if recurrent.

cards.front: What are the indications for surgical management of gastric ulcers?
cards.back:
- Treat complications: bleeding (most common emergency indication), perforation, obstruction
- Refractory to medical management (generally after 8–12 weeks of therapy)
- Suspicion of malignancy (even if biopsy benign), especially if ulcer fails to heal after 12 weeks
Note: Surgery increasingly rare due to H. pylori eradication, PPIs, and endoscopic therapies

Unlike duodenal ulcers, gastric ulcers have a higher risk of malignancy (3× greater risk of obstruction compared to duodenal ulcers). Any gastric ulcer that fails to heal after 12 weeks of medical therapy warrants surgical resection even with a benign biopsy.

cards.front: What surgical procedures are used for gastric and duodenal ulcers?
cards.back:
Gastric ulcers:
- Ligation of bleeding vessels
- Distal gastrectomy with ulcer excision: Billroth II, Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy, or Billroth I
- Vagotomy and pyloroplasty only if acid hypersecretion (very rare)
- Wedge resection if possible

Duodenal ulcers:
- Omental (Graham) patch: plication of perforated ulcer + omental patch
- Oversewing of bleeding ulcer + pyloroplasty
- Post-op H. pylori eradication protocol

The Graham patch is the most common emergency procedure for perforated duodenal ulcer. Post-operative H. pylori eradication is essential to prevent recurrence. Billroth II and Roux-en-Y are preferred over Billroth I for gastric ulcers due to lower tension.

cards.front: What are the complications of duodenal ulceration, their presentations, and management?
cards.back:
Perforation (anterior surface): Sudden-onset pain (may track to RLQ), acute abdomen, CXR showing free air under diaphragm → oversew ulcer (Graham patch)

Penetration (into pancreas/liver): Elevated amylase/lipase, elevated LFTs, constant mid-epigastric pain radiating to back

Hemorrhage (posterior surface — gastroduodenal artery): Resuscitation, endoscopy (laser/cautery/injection), IR angiography with embolization, surgery if refractory
