Contraindication: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)

Primary hyperparathyroidism from a parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of asymptomatic hypercalcemia in outpatients. Preoperative localization uses technetium-99m sestamibi scanning with SPECT, U/S, and contrast CT. Complications include RLN/superior laryngeal nerve injury, postoperative hypocalcemia, infection, and bleeding.

cards.front: What is an adrenal incidentaloma and what are the most common causes?
cards.back:
An adrenal incidentaloma is an adrenal mass >1 cm diameter discovered incidentally during investigation for unrelated symptoms.

Causes by frequency:
- Benign adenoma: 70-80%
- Metastases to adrenal: ~22%
- Cyst, carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, neuroblastoma: rare

Metastasis to adrenal: Lung > Breast > Colon > Lymphoma > Melanoma > Kidney

Peak incidence of carcinoma: females ages 50-60.

All adrenal incidentalomas require biochemical workup to rule out hormonal hypersecretion before any invasive testing. FNA biopsy is generally NOT appropriate because pheochromocytoma must be excluded first (can cause hypertensive crisis during biopsy). CT is the best imaging: size >4-6 cm is the best predictor of primary adrenal carcinoma (92% are >6 cm).

cards.front: What investigations are required for an adrenal incidentaloma?
cards.back:
CT: Size >4-6 cm best predictor of primary adrenal carcinoma (92% are >6 cm); MRI not needed after CT

Functional studies:
- Pheochromocytoma: plasma metanephrines (highly specific and sensitive); if unavailable, 24-h urine catecholamines
- Cushing's: 24-h urine cortisol OR 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test
- Aldosteronoma: electrolytes, AM aldosterone, AM plasma renin activity, ARR (Aldosterone-Renin-Ratio); if inconclusive, saline suppression test
- Adrenal androgens (17-OH progesterone and DHEAS): only if clinical suspicion

FNA biopsy: NOT appropriate in most cases

Pheochromocytoma must be excluded before any procedure including FNA, as it can cause life-threatening hypertensive crisis. Plasma metanephrines are the preferred initial test. Cushing's syndrome from adrenal adenoma is often subclinical. Conn's syndrome (primary aldosteronism) is increasingly recognized as a cause of resistant hypertension.

cards.front: What is the management of a non-functional adrenal incidentaloma based on size?
cards.back:
- >4 cm: Consider resection
- <4 cm: Follow-up imaging in 6-12 months; resect if >1 cm enlargement

Functional tumour: Always resect (regardless of size)

Note: Genetic testing is important for ALL pheochromocytoma/paragangliomas as >30% are related to genetic syndromes.

The size threshold reflects the risk of malignancy — adrenal carcinoma is rare but aggressive. Functional tumours carry additional risk from hormonal excess regardless of malignant potential. Pheochromocytoma surgery requires careful preoperative alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis.

cards.front: What is Whipple's triad and what condition does it characterize?
cards.back:
Whipple's triad characterizes insulinoma:
1. Symptomatic fasting hypoglycemia
2. Serum glucose <2.8 mmol/L
3. Relief of symptoms when glucose is administered

Associated symptoms: palpitations, trembling, diaphoresis, confusion, seizure, personality changes.

Insulinoma is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm. Only 10% are malignant. 10% are associated with MEN1 syndrome. Investigations show decreased serum glucose with elevated serum insulin, C-peptide, and pro-insulin. CT, EUS, and MRI show insulinomas evenly distributed throughout head, body, and tail of the pancreas.

cards.front: What is the treatment for insulinoma?
cards.back:
- Enucleation of solitary insulinomas (may be done endoscopically)
- Tumours >2 cm located close to the pancreatic duct may require pancreatectomy or pancreaticoduodenectomy
- Only 10% are malignant
- 10% are associated with MEN1 (screen for other MEN1 manifestations)

Insulinoma is the most common surgically curable cause of fasting hypoglycemia. Most are benign, solitary, and <2 cm. EUS is particularly useful for localization. Intraoperative ultrasound helps identify small lesions. Medical management with diazoxide can temporize symptoms before surgery.

cards.front: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and how is gastrinoma diagnosed?
cards.back:
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: caused by gastrinoma (tumour secreting gastrin) → excess gastric acid → PUD, severe esophagitis, multiple ulcers in atypical locations refractory to antacid therapy, diarrhea.

Associated with MEN1.

Diagnosis:
- Serum gastrin usually >1000 pg/mL
- Secretin stimulation test
- Endoscopy: 90% develop peptic ulcers
- CT/EUS/MRI: 70-90% in Passaro's triangle (head of pancreas medially, 2nd duodenum inferiorly, confluence of cystic and CBD superiorly)
- Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy scan

Passaro's triangle (gastrinoma triangle) is the key anatomical landmark. 50% of gastrinomas are malignant. High-dose PPI controls acid hypersecretion. Surgical resection is preferred when localized. Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) is used for non-surgical candidates or metastatic disease.

cards.front: What are the clinical features of a VIPoma (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide-secreting tumour)?
cards.back:
- Severe watery diarrhea causing dehydration
- Anorexia and weakness
- Electrolyte imbalance: hypokalemia
- Also known as WDHA syndrome (Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, Achlorhydria) or Verner-Morrison syndrome
- Commonly located in distal pancreas
- Most are malignant

VIPoma is diagnosed by elevated serum VIP levels plus CT/MRI/EUS for localization. Treatment involves fluid and electrolyte repletion, somatostatin analogues (octreotide) for symptom control, and surgical resection or palliative debulking. The massive secretory diarrhea can be life-threatening due to severe dehydration.

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis and what is the diagnostic finding?
cards.back:
Classic presentation:
- Age 6-8 weeks (can present 1-20 weeks)
- M:F = 4:1
- Projectile, non-bilious vomiting 30-60 min after feeds
- Hungry after vomiting
- Visible left-to-right gastric contraction waves after feeding
- Dehydration of variable severity
- Palpable smooth oblong 1-2 cm 'olive' mass in RUQ above umbilicus

Metabolic derangement: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria

Diagnosis: U/S (pyloric length ≥17 mm, muscle thickness >4 mm)

Paradoxical aciduria occurs because volume depletion triggers renal sodium retention; hydrogen ions are exchanged for sodium in the collecting duct despite systemic alkalosis. Treatment requires fluid resuscitation with NS (correct alkalosis first), then pyloromyotomy (Ramstedt procedure — open, transumbilical, or laparoscopic). Surgery should not proceed until metabolic abnormalities are corrected.

cards.front: What is the immediate management priority for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.back:
1. Fluid resuscitation with normal saline (NS)
2. Correct hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with D5, 1/2NS + 20 mEq/L KCl at maintenance rate
3. NG tube decompression (not necessary)
4. Correct electrolyte and acid/base abnormalities BEFORE surgery
5. Then: Pyloromyotomy (Ramstedt procedure) — curative

Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency requiring metabolic correction before surgical intervention. Proceeding with pyloromyotomy before correcting alkalosis risks respiratory depression from anesthesia. The alkalotic state can impair respiratory compensation and cause postoperative apnea. Pyloromyotomy is the definitive treatment; alternative therapies (TPN, atropine) are impractical.

cards.front: What are the key features of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)?
cards.back:
Types: Posterolateral (Bochdalek) — most common; Left-sided 85%, Right-sided 13%; Anterior (Morgagni); Hiatus

Epidemiology: 1 in 2000-5000 live births; M=F; >10% associated with other congenital anomalies

Presentation: Early respiratory distress, cyanosis, scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in chest, displaced heart sounds

Key investigations: CXR (bowel loops in chest, shifted heart), ABG, echocardiography

Treatment: Intubate/ventilate → period of respiratory stabilization (for pulmonary hypertension) → surgical repair (hernia reduction + diaphragm closure)

Prognosis: Neurodevelopmental impairment; hearing deficit (40%); associated GERD

CDH causes pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension — the main causes of mortality. Stabilization before surgery is critical; premature surgery in an unstable patient worsens outcomes. ECMO may be required for severe pulmonary hypertension. Better outcomes occur with later presentations (less pulmonary hypoplasia).

cards.front: What is the cardinal sign of malrotation, and what is the emergency treatment?
cards.back:
Cardinal sign: Bilious emesis (especially if abdomen is non-distended)

Emergency treatment: EMERGENT LAPAROTOMY — Ladd procedure:
1. Counterclockwise reduction of midgut volvulus
2. Division of Ladd's bands
3. Division of peritoneal attachments between cecum and abdominal wall
4. Broadening of the mesentery
5. Positioning bowel in non-rotational position (SBO in right abdomen, LBO in left abdomen)
6. ± Appendectomy

Malrotation occurs in 1 in 500 live births; 1/3 present by 1 week of age. Bilious emesis in a neonate is a surgical emergency until volvulus is excluded. Immediate UGI shows dilated duodenum, duodenojejunal segment right of midline. U/S shows 'whirlpool' sign. Mortality is related to length of bowel loss: 10% necrosis = 100% survival; 75% necrosis = 35% survival.

cards.front: How do you differentiate gastroschisis from omphalocele?
cards.back:
Gastroschisis:
- Defect lateral to cord (usually right)
- NO sac covering viscera
- NOT associated with genetic syndromes
- 10% with intestinal atresia
- Bowel may be inflamed, thickened, matted, foreshortened
- Associated with younger maternal age, IUGR, smoking
- >90% survival rate

Omphalocele:
- Defect at umbilical ring, sac PRESENT (amnion, Wharton's jelly, peritoneum) with cord attached
- 30-70% associated with genetic syndromes (Pentalogy of Cantrell, congenital heart disease, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Trisomy 18)
- Associated pulmonary hypoplasia
- 40-70% survival rate

The presence or absence of a sac and the location relative to the umbilicus are the key distinguishing features. Omphalocele's association with genetic syndromes (especially Trisomy 18 and cardiac defects) drives its higher mortality. Both are diagnosed prenatally with elevated MS-AFP. Treatment for omphalocele: small (<2 cm) = primary closure; larger = silver sulfadiazine dressing or Silo pouch.

cards.front: What is Hirschsprung's disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon)?
cards.back:
Definition: Defect in migration of neural crest cells to intestine → aganglionic bowel that fails to peristalse + internal sphincter fails to relax (internal anal sphincter achalasia) → functional/partial mechanical obstruction

Epidemiology: 1 in 5000 births; M:F = 3-4:1 (approaches 1:1 with whole colon involvement)

Presentation: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of life (95% pass within 24 hours), abdominal distension, constipation, bilious emesis, failure to thrive, enterocolitis/sepsis

Key: Starts in rectum and extends proximally; RET mutation in familial cases (<5%)

Diagnosis: Rectal biopsy (gold standard — look for aganglionosis and neural hypertrophy)

The 'squirt/blast sign' on rectal exam (explosive release of stool/gas upon withdrawal of finger) is characteristic. Contrast enema shows narrow rectum with transition zone. Anal manometry is unreliable in infants. Treatment is Duhamel pull-through procedure — resection of aganglionic segment with anastomosis to anus. Postoperative enterocolitis is the main complication.

cards.front: What is the gold standard investigation for Hirschsprung's disease?
cards.back:
Rectal biopsy — looks for:
1. Aganglionosis (absence of ganglion cells)
2. Neural hypertrophy

Other investigations:
- AXR
- Contrast enema: narrow rectum with transition zone
- Anal manometry: unreliable in infants (classic finding is absence of rectoanal inhibitory reflex)

Treatment: Duhamel pull-through procedure (surgical resection of aganglionic segment + anastomosis to anus)

Rectal biopsy is definitive because it directly demonstrates the absence of ganglion cells in Auerbach's (myenteric) and Meissner's (submucosal) plexuses. Suction rectal biopsy can be performed without anesthesia in newborns. Contrast enema helps identify the transition zone but biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

cards.front: What is the classic triad of intussusception and what is the preferred non-operative treatment?
cards.back:
Classic triad:
1. Episodic 'colicky' abdominal pain
2. Vomiting ± bilious
3. Currant-jelly stool (suggests mucosal necrosis and sloughing)

Plus: Sausage-shaped upper abdominal mass on palpation

Non-operative management: Air contrast enema reduction (preferred in hemodynamically stable patients)

Operative: If peritonitis, failed enema reduction, or compromised bowel → open or laparoscopic reduction ± resection

Intussusception is the most common cause of bowel obstruction between 6-36 months. Usually idiopathic (starts at ileocecal junction). Pathologic lead points (Meckel's diverticulum, polyps, lymphoma) more common in older children or with recurrence. 10% recurrence rate after enema reduction. Allow 2 weeks for edema resolution before SBFT to rule out lead points in older children.

cards.front: What is the VACTERL association and which condition is it associated with?
cards.back:
VACTERL association is associated with Tracheoesophageal Fistula (TEF):
- V: Vertebral anomalies
- A: Anal atresia
- C: Cardiac defects
- TE: TracheoEsophageal fistula
- R: Renal anomalies
- L: Limb defects

Associated anomalies present in 50% of TEF cases.

TEF occurs in 1 in 3000-4500 live births due to defect in lateral septation of foregut into esophagus and trachea. Typically occurs with esophageal atresia. History of maternal polyhydramnios is common. Presentation: frothy bubbles of mucus in mouth/nose, coughing/cyanosis with feeds, non-bilious vomiting, respiratory distress. Early surgical ligation prevents lung damage. Complications after repair: esophageal stenosis/strictures at repair site, GERD, poor swallowing.

cards.front: What is the management of cryptorchidism (undescended testes)?
cards.back:
Investigations:
- Infant: U/S, FSH, LH, karyotype, MIS, 17-hydroxyprogesterone
- Older child: LH, FSH, Mullerian inhibiting substance, hCG stimulation test
- Non-palpable testis: exam under anesthesia, exploratory laparoscopy

Treatment:
- hCG to stimulate testosterone production and descent (medical)
- Orchidopexy: especially if undescended by 6 months-2 years

Benefits of orchidopexy:
- Decreased risk of torsion and blunt trauma
- Preserves spermatogenesis if performed by 1 year
- NO effect on malignant potential of testicle

Cryptorchidism affects 2-5% of term males but most descend spontaneously by 6 months. 1% do not spontaneously descend. Retractile testes (hyperactive cremasteric muscle) can be 'milked' into scrotum and are not truly undescended. Orchidopexy does not reduce the increased cancer risk but allows easier surveillance for testicular malignancy.

cards.front: What are the differences between duodenal atresia and jejunoileal atresia in terms of pathophysiology and associations?
cards.back:
Duodenal atresia:
- Pathophysiology: Failure of bowel to recanalize after endodermal epithelium proliferation (weeks 8-10)
- Associated with: Down syndrome (24-28%), tracheoesophageal fistula, cardiac, renal, vertebral anomalies
- X-ray: 'Double-bubble' sign (dilated stomach + duodenum)
- Prognosis: 86% long-term survival
- Treatment: Duodenoduodenostomy or duodenojejunostomy

Jejunoileal atresia:
- Pathophysiology: Vascular disruption → ischemic necrosis → resorption of necrotic tissue
- Associated with: CF
- Prognosis: 84% long-term survival
- Treatment: Primary anastomosis (or end stoma if short bowel)

Colonic atresia:
- 100% long-term survival

The double-bubble sign on X-ray (or prenatal U/S) is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia. All intestinal atresias present with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension within 24-72 hours of birth. Treatment requires NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and TPN before surgical correction.

cards.front: What are the key features of pediatric inguinal hernias?
cards.back:
Epidemiology: 5% of term newborns; M:F = 4:1; 2× risk and more likely bilateral if preterm

Pathophysiology: ALL infant hernias are indirect — descent through internal inguinal ring via patent tunica vaginalis

Presentation: Painless intermittent mass in groin ± extension into scrotum

Risk: 1/5 inguinal hernias will become incarcerated if patient is <1 year old; incarceration more common in females

Management:
- Reducible: repair within a few weeks if <1 year; elective if >1 year
- Incarcerated: repair immediately (emergency); attempt manual reduction in ER first

Treatment: Herniorrhaphy (laparoscopic or open) with high ligation of sac

Recurrence: <3% after repair

The 'silk sign' (palpable thickening of cord over pubic tubercle, like rubbing silk on silk) suggests indirect hernia. Hydrocele (scrotal mass without inguinal mass, transilluminates) must be distinguished — communicating hydroceles increase in size with standing/Valsalva. Always attempt reduction to confirm hernia is not incarcerated before proceeding.

cards.front: What is a communicating versus non-communicating hydrocele in pediatric patients?
cards.back:
Communicating hydrocele:
- Processus vaginalis connects peritoneum with tunica vaginalis
- Peritoneal fluid flows freely between the two
- Potential for contents to enter groin (i.e., inguinal hernia)
- Size increases with standing or Valsalva; absent in morning, large in evening
- 'Silk glove sign': gently palpating hydrocele sac over pubic tubercle feels like rubbing silk on silk

Non-communicating hydrocele:
- Processus vaginalis is closed
- More fluid produced than absorbed in tunica vaginalis
- In older children may be secondary to testicular pathology (reactive hydrocele)

Most resolve spontaneously by 1 year

Hydroceles occur in 1-2% of live births with M:F = 6:1. The key distinguishing feature is whether the processus vaginalis is patent (communicating) or closed (non-communicating). Surgical repair is indicated for: persistence >2 years, pain, fluctuating size (suggesting communication), cosmetic reasons, or infection. Transillumination confirms fluid-filled scrotal mass.

cards.front: What are common DVT prophylaxis regimens used in surgical patients in Canada?
cards.back:
DVT Prophylaxis options:
- Heparin: 5000 units SC BID (non-cancer patient); 5000 units SC TID/BID (cancer patient)
- Dalteparin (Fragmin): 5000 units SC daily
- Enoxaparin (Lovenox): 40 mg SC daily

Cancer patients are at higher VTE risk and require more aggressive prophylaxis. Low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH) like dalteparin and enoxaparin are preferred over unfractionated heparin in most surgical patients due to once-daily dosing and predictable pharmacokinetics. Sequential compression devices (SCDs) are used as mechanical prophylaxis adjuncts.

cards.front: What are the key antibiotic choices for common surgical infections?
cards.back:
Key surgical antibiotics:
- Cefazolin (Ancef): Gram-positive (except Enterococcus), limited Gram-negative (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) — 1g IV/IM perioperative prophylaxis
- Metronidazole (Flagyl): Anaerobes — 500 mg PO/IV BID (TID for C. difficile)
- Piperacillin/tazobactam: GP, GN, and anaerobes — 3.375g IV q6h
- Vancomycin: GP and MRSA — 1g IV q12h
- Ciprofloxacin: GN including Pseudomonas — 400 mg IV q12h or 500 mg PO BID
- Ceftriaxone: Broad coverage including Pseudomonas — 1-2g IM/IV q24h
- Gentamicin: GN including Pseudomonas — 3-5 mg/kg/day divided q8h (monitor creatinine and levels)

Cefazolin is the standard perioperative prophylactic antibiotic for most clean and clean-contaminated surgical procedures. For bowel surgery, coverage should include anaerobes (add metronidazole or use piperacillin/tazobactam). Vancomycin is reserved for MRSA coverage or penicillin allergy. Gentamicin requires monitoring for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

cards.front: What is the adrenal cortex anatomy (zones and hormones)?
cards.back:
From outer to inner (GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex):
- Glomerulosa (outermost): Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)
- Fasciculata (middle): Glucocorticoids (cortisol)
- Reticularis (inner): Sex steroids (androgens)

Adrenal medulla: Catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)

Mnemonic: 'GFR — the deeper you go, the sweeter it gets' (salt → sugar → sex). This zonal organization is important for understanding adrenal tumours: Conn's syndrome (aldosteronoma — glomerulosa), Cushing's syndrome (glucocorticoma — fasciculata), virilizing tumours (reticularis), pheochromocytoma (medulla). Each zone has distinct embryologic origin and regulatory mechanisms.

cards.front: What is the key clinical message from the CHOCOLATE trial regarding acute cholecystitis?
cards.back:
CHOCOLATE trial (BMJ 2018): In high-risk patients with acute calculous cholecystitis, laparoscopic cholecystectomy is SUPERIOR to percutaneous catheter drainage:
- Complication rate: 12% (cholecystectomy) vs. 65% (drainage)
- Drainage group had: higher reintervention rate, more recurrent biliary disease, longer length of stay
- Mortality rate did not differ significantly between groups

Conclusion: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy reduces major complications in high-risk patients with acute cholecystitis compared with percutaneous drainage.

Despite concerns about operating on high-risk patients, this trial showed that definitive surgical treatment (cholecystectomy) had far better outcomes than temporizing with percutaneous drainage. Percutaneous drainage leaves the gallbladder in place, leading to recurrent disease requiring multiple interventions. This supports early cholecystectomy even in higher-risk patients when technically feasible.

cards.front: What are the clinical features and treatment of umbilical hernias in children?
cards.back:
Epidemiology: Incidence 2-11%; increases with prematurity; M:F = 1.5:1

Features:
- Majority asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously by 4 years (95% by age 4)
- Defects >1.5 cm in infancy will not close spontaneously
- Incarceration prior to age 5 is very rare

Treatment:
- Repair if NOT spontaneously closed by age 5
- Earlier repair of large 'proboscoid' hernias with extensive skin stretching (cosmetic reasons)
- Simple primary closure of fascial defect

Recurrence: Low risk

Umbilical hernias result from incomplete closure of peritoneal and fascial layers. They differ from other hernias in that incarceration is rare in childhood. The size of the fascial defect determines chances of spontaneous closure. Most symptoms occur in late adolescence or adulthood if not closed. Unlike epigastric hernias, umbilical hernias usually resolve without intervention.

cards.front: What is the significance of bilious emesis in a neonate?
cards.back:
Bilious emesis in a neonate is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY until proven otherwise.

Main concern: Malrotation with midgut volvulus

Immediate management:
- IV antibiotics and fluid resuscitation
- AXR and immediate UGI series (shows 'corkscrew' sign or dilated duodenum with duodenojejunal segment right of midline)
- U/S: 'whirlpool' sign, abnormal SMA/SMV relationship
- If volvulus confirmed: EMERGENT LAPAROTOMY (Ladd procedure)

Other causes to consider: Intestinal atresia, Hirschsprung's disease, meconium ileus

The non-distended abdomen with bilious emesis is the classic presentation of malrotation with volvulus — the bowel twists around the superior mesenteric artery. Delayed diagnosis leads to massive bowel infarction and short bowel syndrome. Mortality is directly related to the extent of bowel necrosis. Every hour counts — this is a true surgical emergency.

cards.front: What does the 'double-bubble' sign on X-ray indicate and what conditions cause it?
cards.back:
Double-bubble sign: Two gas-filled bubbles — one in stomach and one in proximal duodenum — with no distal gas

Causes:
1. Duodenal atresia (most common)
2. Duodenal stenosis
3. Annular pancreas
4. Ladd's bands (malrotation) compressing duodenum

Association: Duodenal atresia is associated with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) in 24-28% of cases

The double-bubble sign can be seen prenatally on U/S or postnatally on plain AXR. No distal gas distinguishes complete atresia from stenosis (which may have some distal gas). The clinical presentation is bilious vomiting shortly after birth. Duodenal atresia results from failure of recanalization during bowel development (weeks 8-10), distinct from the vascular disruption mechanism of jejunoileal atresia.

cards.front: What percentage of thyroid lobectomy and total thyroidectomy patients require thyroxine replacement?
cards.back:
- Lobectomy: 20-75% of patients need thyroxine after lobectomy
- Total thyroidectomy: 100% of patients need thyroxine after total thyroidectomy

The wide range for lobectomy (20-75%) reflects variable function of the remaining lobe; patients with pre-existing subclinical hypothyroidism or Hashimoto's thyroiditis are more likely to require replacement. After total thyroidectomy, permanent thyroxine replacement is mandatory. TSH monitoring guides appropriate dosing — over-replacement increases fracture risk and can cause AF.

cards.front: What is the role of neoadjuvant therapy in Stage III breast cancer?
cards.back:
Stage IIIA-IIIC breast cancer:
- Primary treatment: Likely mastectomy + axillary node dissection + radiotherapy after chemotherapy (neoadjuvant)
- Neoadjuvant (preoperative) therapy should be considered especially if not immediately resectable
- Goals of neoadjuvant therapy:
  1. Downstage tumour to achieve resectability
  2. Assess tumour chemosensitivity in vivo
  3. Eradicate micrometastases
- Adjuvant radiation and chemotherapy may also be appropriate postoperatively

Inflammatory breast cancer:
- Mastectomy + axillary node dissection + radiotherapy
- Neoadjuvant therapy is standard

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced breast cancer allows assessment of pathological complete response (pCR), which is a strong prognostic indicator. In HER2-positive disease, adding trastuzumab + pertuzumab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy significantly improves pCR rates. Inflammatory breast cancer (T4d) requires systemic therapy before any surgery.

cards.front: What is the Meckel scan and what does it detect?
cards.back:
Meckel scan (Tc-99m pertechnetate scan):
- Detects ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum
- Technetium-99m pertechnetate is taken up by gastric mucosa (parietal cells)
- Sensitivity: 85%
- Specificity: 95%

Alternative imaging: AXR (may show lower abdominal tenderness/distension)

Indication: Painless BRBPR (bright red blood per rectum) in a child near the umbilicus, especially if <5 years old

Only the 50% of Meckel's diverticula that contain ectopic gastric mucosa are detectable by this scan. False negatives occur when gastric mucosa is absent. False positives can occur with other conditions that uptake pertechnetate. The scan is performed IV and images are taken sequentially. Treatment is surgical resection by laparotomy or laparoscopy + incidental appendectomy.

cards.front: What are the common surgical analgesic options and their dosing?
cards.back:
Surgical analgesics:
- Acetaminophen + codeine (Tylenol #3): 1-2 tabs q4-6h PO/PR prn
- Hydromorphone: 1-2 tabs PO q4h prn; 0.5-2 mg IV q3-4h prn
- Ibuprofen: 200-400 mg PO q4-6h prn
- Morphine: 2.5-10 mg IM/SC q4-6h prn; 1-2 mg IV q1h prn for breakthrough
- Ketorolac (Toradol): 30-60 mg IM/IV q6h prn
- Acetaminophen/oxycodone (Percocet): 325/5 mg, 1-2 tabs PO q4-6h prn

Multimodal analgesia (combining non-opioid agents with opioids) reduces opioid requirements and side effects. NSAIDs (ibuprofen, ketorolac) provide anti-inflammatory analgesia but should be used cautiously in patients with renal impairment, peptic ulcer disease, or post-GI surgery. Ketorolac is the parenteral NSAID option for moderate-severe pain.

cards.front: What is the treatment approach for metastatic (Stage IV) breast cancer?
cards.back:
Stage IV (any T, any N, M1):
- Primary treatment is systemic therapy: chemotherapy and/or hormone therapy
- Surgery: as appropriate for local control only
- Radiation: palliative
- Overall survival: 36-60 months (not curable)

Metastatic sites in order: Bone > Lungs > Pleura > Liver > Brain

Stage IV breast cancer is treated with palliative intent. Treatment selection depends on ER/PR/HER2 status, prior therapy, performance status, and sites of metastasis. Bone-directed therapy (bisphosphonates, denosumab) is used for bone metastases. Targeted therapies (CDK4/6 inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors) have expanded options for ER-positive metastatic disease in Canadian practice.

cards.front: What is the most commonly used arterial graft for coronary artery bypass surgery, and should it be skeletonized?
cards.back:
Internal thoracic artery (ITA); skeletonization is debated but may reduce sternal blood supply

Studies by Athanasiou et al. examined whether skeletonization of the internal thoracic artery affects outcomes in CABG surgery.

cards.front: What does the Ross procedure involve, and what are its long-term outcomes?
cards.back:
The Ross procedure involves using the patient's own pulmonary autograft to replace the aortic valve; long-term outcomes show favorable results but require reoperation for the pulmonary homograft

Studies by Aboud et al. showed long-term outcomes of patients undergoing the Ross procedure with generally good results.

cards.front: What is the preferred surgical treatment for achalasia compared to medical therapy?
cards.back:
Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) or laparoscopic Heller myotomy - 83% success rate at 2 years

NEJM 2019 study showed POEM was non-inferior to laparoscopic Heller myotomy with 83% clinical success vs 81.7%, significantly better than medical treatment.

cards.front: What is the POEM procedure and how does it compare to laparoscopic Heller myotomy?
cards.back:
POEM (peroral endoscopic myotomy) is as effective as laparoscopic Heller myotomy for achalasia at 2 years (83% vs 81.7% clinical success)

A 2019 NEJM study showed POEM achieved clinical success in 83% vs 81.7% for LHM at 2 years, demonstrating non-inferiority.

cards.front: What is indicated before surgical fundoplication?
cards.back:
Esophageal manometry to ensure intact esophageal function

Esophageal manometry is indicated before surgical fundoplication to ensure intact esophageal function and exclude alternative diagnoses like scleroderma and achalasia.

cards.front: What is an aortoenteric fistula and why is it a surgical emergency?
cards.back:
A rare and lethal cause of GI bleed, most common in patients with history of aortic graft surgery. Requires emergency surgery as the window of opportunity is narrow.

Aortoenteric fistulas create direct communication between the aorta and intestinal lumen, causing massive bleeding. Suspect in patients with aortic grafts presenting with abdominal pain and bleeding.

cards.front: What is the role of esophageal manometry before fundoplication?
cards.back: To ensure intact esophageal function and exclude alternative diagnoses like scleroderma and achalasia

cards.front: What are the indications for placing surgical drains?
cards.back:
To prevent fluid accumulation (blood, pus, serum, bile, urine), to assess third space fluid accumulation postoperatively, and to provide a route for drainage.

Drains are placed selectively at surgery to prevent complications from fluid accumulation and to monitor postoperative output.

cards.front: What are the three main categories of surgical drains?
cards.back:
Open (e.g., Penrose), closed (gravity like Foley, underwater-seal like chest tube, suction like Jackson-Pratt), and sump drains (e.g., NG tube).

Drains are categorized by their mechanism: open drains have higher infection risk, closed drains use gravity or suction, and sump drains provide active suction.

cards.front: What special precaution should be taken for all neck surgery patients?
cards.back:
Have a suture kit at bedside in all neck surgery patients in case of emergent hematoma requiring immediate decompression.

Given the risk of airway compromise from neck hematoma, having emergency equipment immediately available can be life-saving.

cards.front: What procedure repairs obstructed UPJ (ureteropelvic junction)?
cards.back:
Pyeloplasty

Pyeloplasty is the surgical correction of UPJ obstruction, whether congenital or acquired.

cards.front: What did the CLEAR III trial (Lancet 2017) find regarding alteplase irrigation for intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) via EVD?
cards.back:
Alteplase 1mg q8h (up to 12 doses) via EVD did NOT significantly improve functional outcomes (mRS ≤3 at 180 days) compared to saline irrigation (48% vs 45%; RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.88–1.28; P=0.554).

The CLEAR III trial studied 500 patients with non-traumatic ICH <30mL + IVH obstructing the 3rd/4th ventricles. Despite pharmacological clot lysis, functional outcomes were equivalent. Alteplase should NOT be used routinely for IVH via EVD.

cards.front: What did the MRC CRASH trial (Lancet 2004) establish about corticosteroids in traumatic brain injury?
cards.back:
Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 48h infusion) significantly INCREASED the risk of death (P=0.0001) in patients with head injury (GCS <14). Corticosteroids should NOT be used to treat head injury of any severity.

10,008 patients with head injury were randomized. Corticosteroid use was harmful across all injury severities and time-since-injury subgroups. This trial definitively ended routine steroid use in TBI management.

cards.front: What were the key findings of the DECRA trial (NEJM 2011) regarding decompressive craniectomy in diffuse TBI?
cards.back:
In 155 patients with severe diffuse TBI and refractory ICP, early bifrontotemporoparietal decompressive craniectomy reduced ICP and ICU stay but was associated with POORER Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale scores (P=0.03) and greater risk of unfavourable outcomes (P=0.02) vs. standard care.

While craniectomy successfully lowered ICP, it did not translate into better functional outcomes—paradoxically outcomes were worse. This challenged the assumption that ICP control alone improves prognosis in diffuse TBI.

cards.front: What did the BEST:TRIP trial (NEJM 2012) conclude about ICP monitoring vs. imaging/clinical examination in severe TBI?
cards.back:
In 324 patients with severe TBI, care guided by ICP monitoring was NO better than care based on imaging and clinical examination alone for the composite primary outcome (survival, consciousness, functional status, neuropsychological status at 3–6 months).

BEST:TRIP was conducted in South America and challenged the routine use of ICP monitors in severe TBI management. It showed that experienced clinical teams using imaging-based protocols achieved equivalent outcomes, though criticisms included differences in ICU practice context.

cards.front: What did the POLAR trial (JAMA 2018) find about prophylactic hypothermia in severe TBI?
cards.back:
Prophylactic hypothermia (33–35°C for ≥72h and <7 days) did NOT improve 6-month neurologic outcomes (GOS-E score 5–8) compared to normothermia (48.8% vs 49.7%; RR 0.99; P=0.94) in 511 patients with severe TBI.

Despite physiologic rationale for neuroprotection, prophylactic cooling after severe TBI confers no functional benefit. This is consistent with prior negative hypothermia trials (NABIS:H II, Eurotherm). Current guidelines do not recommend prophylactic hypothermia for TBI.

cards.front: In the Shunt Design Trial (Neurosurgery 1998) for pediatric hydrocephalus, which valve type performed best?
cards.back:
There was NO significant difference in shunt failure-free duration among the standard differential-pressure valve, Delta valve, or Orbis-Sigma valve (P=0.24). 61% were shunt failure-free at 1 year and 47% at 2 years.

344 hydrocephalic children undergoing first shunt insertion were randomized to three valve types. Anti-siphon and flow-control valves designed to limit overdrainage provided no advantage over standard valves, guiding simplified shunt selection.

cards.front: How does endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) compare to CSF shunting in pediatric hydrocephalus over time?
cards.back:
ETV has a HIGHER initial failure rate than shunts (first ~3 months), but after 3 months the relative risk of failure progressively favours ETV, suggesting a long-term survival benefit over shunting.

This propensity-score adjusted cohort analysis demonstrated that ETV's early failure risk is offset by superior long-term patency. ETV is now preferred for obstructive hydrocephalus in appropriate candidates, avoiding the lifelong shunt dependency and revision burden.

cards.front: What did the randomized trial of surgery for temporal-lobe epilepsy (NEJM 2001) demonstrate?
cards.back:
Surgery was vastly superior to antiepileptic drug therapy: 58% of surgical patients were seizure-free (awareness-impairing seizures) vs. only 8% in the medical group (P<0.001), with significantly better quality of life.

80 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy were randomized to surgery vs. 1 year of continued medical therapy. This landmark trial established early surgical referral as the standard of care for drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy rather than prolonged medication trials.

cards.front: What did the PROCESS trial (Pain 2007) find about spinal cord stimulation (SCS) for failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS)?
cards.back:
SCS plus conventional medical management (CMM) achieved ≥50% leg pain relief in 48% vs. 9% with CMM alone (P<0.001), with improved quality of life and function. 32% of SCS patients experienced device-related complications at 12 months.

100 FBSS patients with neuropathic radicular leg pain were randomized. SCS is now an evidence-based treatment for FBSS when conservative measures fail. The high complication rate (32%) underscores the need for careful patient selection and technical expertise.

cards.front: What did the EARLYSTIM trial (NEJM 2013) establish about deep brain stimulation (DBS) timing in Parkinson's disease?
cards.back:
DBS (neurostimulation) in early-stage Parkinson's disease improved quality of life by 7.8 points vs. a 0.2-point worsening with medical therapy alone (P=0.002), with benefits in motor function, ADLs, and dyskinesia. Serious surgical adverse events occurred in 17.7%.

EARLYSTIM challenged the practice of reserving DBS for advanced disease. Earlier neurostimulation provides superior quality of life outcomes, supporting consideration of DBS when early motor complications emerge rather than waiting for disease progression.

cards.front: What did the focused ultrasound thalamotomy RCT (NEJM 2016) demonstrate for essential tremor?
cards.back:
Unilateral MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy improved hand tremor scores by 8.3 points more than sham (95% CI 5.9–10.7; P<0.001) at 3 months, with sustained improvement at 12 months (7.2-point change from baseline).

76 patients with refractory moderate-to-severe essential tremor were randomized. This non-invasive treatment targets the ventral intermediate nucleus (VIM) of the thalamus, providing a therapeutic alternative to DBS or conventional surgical thalamotomy without craniotomy.

cards.front: What did the landmark trial on surgery vs. XRT for metastatic spinal cord compression (Lancet 2005) show?
cards.back:
Direct decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy (XRT) was superior to XRT alone: 84% vs. 57% of patients could walk after treatment (OR 6.2; P=0.001) in 101 patients with metastatic spinal cord compression.

This Patchell et al. trial established that for patients with radiographically confirmed metastatic spinal cord compression and expected survival >3 months, direct decompressive surgery + XRT is the standard of care, significantly improving ambulatory function.

cards.front: What did the SPORT trial 8-year results (Spine 2014) show about surgery vs. non-operative treatment for lumbar disc herniation?
cards.back:
In intention-to-treat analysis, open discectomy was superior for sciatica severity (P=0.005), patient satisfaction (P=0.013), and self-rated improvement (P=0.013) at 8 years. Pain/function/disability benefits were only demonstrated in as-treated analysis due to high cross-over rates.

501 patients with confirmed lumbar disc herniation were randomized. The high cross-over rate (many non-surgical patients eventually had surgery) limited the ITT analysis. The as-treated analysis favoured surgery. Carefully selected surgical candidates derive meaningful long-term benefit.

cards.front: What did the SPORT 8-year results for lumbar spinal stenosis (Spine 2015) demonstrate about decompressive laminectomy?
cards.back:
Decompressive laminectomy showed early benefits over non-operative care until ~4 years, but primary outcome differences converged between years 5–8. Symptomatic benefits of surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis may diminish beyond 4 years.

289 patients were randomized (laminectomy vs. non-operative care). The 52% crossover rate in the non-operative group limited ITT analysis. Clinicians should set realistic expectations with patients—surgical benefits for stenosis are meaningful but may not be permanent.

cards.front: What did the STASCIS study (PLoS ONE 2012) find about timing of surgical decompression for traumatic cervical SCI?
cards.back:
Early surgical decompression (<24h) was associated with greater neurological recovery: odds of ≥2 AIS grade improvement were 2.83 times higher with early vs. late surgery (95% CI 1.10–7.28), with no significant difference in complication rates (P=0.21).

313 patients with cervical SCI at 6 North American institutions were studied. STASCIS was foundational evidence establishing <24h decompression as the target timeframe for cervical SCI, now reflected in Canadian and international clinical guidelines.

cards.front: What did the pooled analysis on timing of decompression for acute SCI (Lancet Neurology 2021) confirm?
cards.back:
Early surgery (<24h) in 528 patients resulted in greater 1-year motor recovery (+23.7 points) vs. late surgery in 1020 patients (+19.7 points), MD 4.0 points (P=0.0006), with similar improvements in light touch and pin prick scores. The critical window is the first 24–36h.

This large pooled analysis of 4 prospective multicenter datasets (1991–2017) confirms that the first 24–36h after acute SCI is the optimal window for decompressive surgery to maximize sensorimotor recovery—aligned with STASCIS and current guidelines.

cards.front: What did the RCT on ventral vs. dorsal surgery for cervical spondylotic myelopathy (JAMA 2021) conclude?
cards.back:
Ventral and dorsal surgery achieved equivalent improvement in patient-reported physical functioning at 1 year (5.9 vs. 6.2 points on SF-36 PCS; mean difference 0.3; 95% CI −2.6 to 3.1; P=0.86) in 163 patients with multilevel cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

Surgical approach selection (anterior vs. posterior) for multilevel CSM should be individualized based on anatomy, pathology pattern, and surgeon expertise, as both approaches yield equivalent functional outcomes. This supports flexibility in surgical planning.

cards.front: What did the CSM-Protect trial (Lancet 2021) find about riluzole in degenerative cervical myelopathy?
cards.back:
Riluzole (50mg twice daily, perioperative) did NOT enhance functional recovery beyond decompressive surgery alone. No difference in modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score change was found (difference −0.38 points; P=0.14) in 290 patients.

Riluzole, a glutamate antagonist approved for ALS, was hypothesized to provide neuroprotection during surgical decompression for degenerative cervical myelopathy. This phase 3 RCT found no benefit, ruling out riluzole as adjuvant therapy for CSM.

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.back:
Sudden onset (seconds) 'thunderclap' headache described as the 'worst headache of my life,' usually after exertion. Associated with N/V, photophobia, meningismus, and decreased LOC.

SAH is caused by ruptured aneurysm in 75-80% of spontaneous cases. CT without contrast is 98% sensitive within 12 hours. If CT is negative but suspicion is high, LP should be performed looking for xanthochromia and elevated RBCs. ~30-60% of patients have a prior sentinel bleed.

cards.front: What are the most common locations for saccular (berry) aneurysms?
cards.back:
Anterior communicating artery (30%), posterior communicating artery (25%), middle cerebral artery (20%), basilar tip (7%).

85-95% are in the carotid (anterior) system. Risk factors include smoking, HTN, adult polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history. Rupture risk increases with size; unruptured aneurysms >10 mm are generally treated.

cards.front: What is vasospasm after SAH and how is it managed?
cards.back:
Vasoconstriction causing delayed cerebral ischemia, onset 4-14 days post-SAH (peak 6-8 days). Treatment: nimodipine (neuroprotection), hyperdynamic therapy (fluids and pressors after aneurysm secured), and angioplasty for refractory cases.

Nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h x 21 days is the only validated neuroprotective agent. Symptomatic vasospasm occurs in 20-30% of SAH patients. Risk factors include large amount of blood on CT (high Fisher grade), smoking, and older age. DCI is a major cause of morbidity after SAH.

cards.front: What is the classic sequence of epidural hematoma presentation?
cards.back:
Post-traumatic reduced LOC → lucid interval of several hours → obtundation, hemiparesis, ipsilateral pupillary dilation → coma.

This classic 'talk and die' presentation is seen in <30% of cases. Most epidural hematomas are from ruptured middle meningeal artery after temporal-parietal skull fracture. CT shows lenticular-shaped hyperdensity. Urgent craniotomy is needed unless the clot is small (<30 mL), thin (<15 mm), with minimal midline shift and GCS >8.

cards.front: What is the ICH score used for and what are its components?
cards.back:
Predicts mortality in intracerebral hemorrhage. Components: GCS (13-15=0, 5-12=1, 3-4=2), ICH volume (≥30 cm³=1), presence of IVH (yes=1), infratentorial origin (yes=1), age ≥80 (yes=1).

ICH accounts for ~10% of strokes with 44% 30-day mortality. HTN is the most common cause (bleeds at putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum). Treatment includes BP reduction to 140/90, reversal of anticoagulation, ICP control, and seizure prophylaxis. Corticosteroids should NOT be used.

cards.front: What is the Spetzler-Martin AVM grading scale?
cards.back:
Points for: Size (<3cm=1, 3-6cm=2, >6cm=3), location (non-eloquent=0, eloquent=1), and venous drainage (superficial=0, deep=1). Grades I-II are surgical candidates; higher grades have more risk.

AVMs are tangles of abnormal vessels with arteriovenous shunts and no intervening capillary beds. They present with hemorrhage (40-60%), seizures (50%), and steal phenomena. Untreated, they carry a 2-4% annual risk of major bleed. Treatment options include surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, and embolization.

cards.front: What is the approach to cerebral abscess management?
cards.back:
Aspiration/excision with Gram stain and C&S, empiric antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole for 6-8 weeks), anticonvulsants for 1-2 years, and follow-up with MRI.

Streptococcus is the most common pathogen. The abscess shows ring enhancement on CT and restricted diffusion on MRI (DWI positive, ADC dark — distinguishes from tumor which is ADC bright). Mortality is ~10% with appropriate therapy but 50% have permanent deficits.

cards.front: What is the rebleed risk after SAH and how is it prevented?
cards.back:
4% on day 1, 15-20% within 2 weeks, 50% by 6 months. Prevention: early clipping or coiling of the aneurysm (within 48-96 hours).

Rebleeding is a major cause of mortality after SAH. Per the ISAT trial, endovascular coiling showed greater survival benefit at 1 year compared to clipping for ruptured aneurysms suitable for both treatments, with the benefit sustained at 10 years. However, rebleeding was slightly more common with coiling.

cards.front: What are the red flags for back pain suggesting serious pathology (mnemonic BACK PAIN)?
cards.back:
B: Bowel/Bladder dysfunction. A: Anesthesia (saddle). C: Constitutional symptoms. K: Khronic disease. P: Paresthesia. A: Age >50 or <20. I: IV drug use. N: Neuromotor deficits.

Cauda equina syndrome (urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness) is a surgical emergency. Malignancy red flags include age >50, cancer history, and pain unrelieved by bed rest. Infection red flags include elevated ESR, IVDU, and fever.

cards.front: What chronic SDH presentation makes it the 'great imitator'?
cards.back:
Presents with global rather than focal deficits: progressive dementia, confusion, gait problems, minor headaches, lightheadedness, and TIA-like symptoms. Can mimic dementia, tumors, and other conditions.

Chronic SDH occurs ≥15 days after bleeding onset, often in elderly patients, alcoholics, and those on anticoagulants. CT shows hypodense crescentic collection crossing suture lines. Treatment is burr hole drainage of liquefied clot if symptomatic or >1 cm thick.

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of an epidural hematoma?
cards.back:
Post-traumatic loss of consciousness, followed by a lucid interval of several hours, then rapid deterioration with obtundation, contralateral hemiparesis, and ipsilateral pupillary dilation.

The classic 'lucid interval' is seen in <30% of cases. 85% are caused by ruptured middle meningeal artery from temporal-parietal skull fracture. CT shows a lenticular (biconvex) hyperdense mass limited by suture lines. This is a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent craniotomy. Prognosis is good with prompt treatment.

cards.front: How do you differentiate an epidural hematoma from a subdural hematoma on CT?
cards.back:
Epidural: lenticular (biconvex) shape, limited by suture lines, usually from arterial bleeding (middle meningeal artery). Subdural: crescentic shape, crosses suture lines, usually from ruptured bridging veins.

Epidural hematomas are typically associated with skull fracture and have a better prognosis when treated promptly because the underlying brain is often undamaged. Acute subdural hematomas have 40-60% mortality because the brain parenchyma is often injured. Chronic SDH is hypodense on CT.

cards.front: What are the risk factors for chronic subdural hematoma?
cards.back:
Advanced age, alcoholism, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, CSF shunts, coagulopathies, cerebral atrophy, and shaken baby syndrome.

Chronic SDH develops >15 days after bleeding onset, often from minor or no recalled injuries. It is called 'the great imitator' because it can mimic dementia, tumors, or TIA. Treatment is burr hole drainage of the liquefied clot. Postoperative subdural drains reduce recurrence (RR 0.45).

cards.front: What is the hallmark presentation of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.back:
Sudden onset (seconds) of severe 'thunderclap headache,' described as the 'worst headache of my life,' usually following exertion, accompanied by meningismus, nausea/vomiting, and decreased LOC.

SAH is most commonly caused by trauma; spontaneous SAH is 75-80% due to ruptured aneurysms. Non-contrast CT is 98% sensitive within 12 hours. If CT is negative but suspicion is high, perform LP (xanthochromic CSF). Sentinel bleeds precede full SAH in 30-60% of patients within 3 weeks.

cards.front: What is the most common location for saccular (berry) aneurysms?
cards.back:
Anterior communicating artery (30%), followed by internal carotid/posterior communicating artery (25-30%) and middle cerebral artery (20%).

Saccular aneurysms are the most common type, located at branch points of the circle of Willis. 85-95% are in the anterior circulation. Risk factors include HTN, smoking, polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history. 20-30% of patients have multiple aneurysms.

cards.front: What is vasospasm after SAH, and when does it peak?
cards.back:
Vasoconstriction and pathological vascular changes in response to blood irritation of vessels, onset 4-14 days post-SAH, peaking at 6-8 days. Symptomatic in 20-30% of patients.

Vasospasm can lead to delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) and death. Risk factors include large blood load on CT (high Fisher grade), smoking, age, and HTN. Treatment: hyperdynamic therapy (fluids + pressors) after aneurysm securing, angioplasty or intra-arterial verapamil for refractory cases. Nimodipine 60 mg q4h x 21d is the only validated neuroprotective agent.

cards.front: What is nimodipine's role in SAH management?
cards.back:
It is the only validated neuroprotective agent for delayed cerebral ischemia post-SAH. Dose: 60 mg PO/NG q4h for 21 days.

Although nimodipine is a calcium channel blocker, its benefit in SAH is through neuroprotection rather than vasodilation. IV magnesium and clazosentan reduce DCI and vasospasm respectively but have not shown functional outcome benefit. Statins also showed no neuroprotective benefit in trials.

cards.front: What are the most common locations for hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
cards.back:
Basal ganglia/internal capsule (50%), thalamus (15%), cerebral white matter (15%), cerebellum (5%), and pons (15%).

ICH accounts for ~10% of strokes with 44% 30-day mortality. Clinical features include gradual onset of symptoms during activity, headache, N/V, and decreased LOC. CT shows hyperdense intraparenchymal blood. Medical treatment targets BP reduction (MAP target ~140/90), ICP control, and coagulopathy reversal.

cards.front: What is the most common organism causing cerebral abscess?
cards.back:
Streptococcus species (often anaerobic or microaerophilic).

Cerebral abscess can arise via hematogenous spread (chest source most common in adults), direct implantation, contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis media), or from PNS. 10-60% have no identifiable cause. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is the imaging modality of choice. Treatment: aspiration/excision + empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole for 6-8 weeks.

cards.front: How does MRI differentiate a cerebral abscess from a brain tumor?
cards.back:
On diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), abscess shows restriction (bright on DWI, dark on ADC map), while tumor appears white on ADC map.

Both abscess and tumor can show ring enhancement on contrast-enhanced MRI. The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map is the key distinguishing feature: abscess appears black (restricted diffusion due to viscous pus) while tumor appears white (facilitated diffusion). Lymphoma can also show restriction on DWI.

cards.front: What are the components and scores of the Glasgow Coma Scale?
cards.back:
Eye opening (1-4): spontaneous=4, to voice=3, to pain=2, none=1. Verbal (1-5): oriented=5, confused=4, inappropriate=3, incomprehensible=2, none=1. Motor (1-6): obeys=6, localizes=5, withdraws=4, flexion/decorticate=3, extension/decerebrate=2, none=1. Total: 3-15.

GCS is used to classify TBI severity: mild (13-15), moderate (9-12), severe (<8). GCS <8 is an indication for intubation. The motor score is the most predictive component for outcomes. Each component should be recorded individually (e.g., E3V3M5).

cards.front: What are the criteria for the Canadian CT Head Rule in minor head injury?
cards.back:
CT required if any: GCS <15 at 2h, suspected open/depressed skull fracture, any sign of basilar skull fracture, vomiting >=2 episodes, age >=65. Medium risk: retrograde amnesia >30 min, dangerous mechanism.

Minor head injury is defined as witnessed LOC, amnesia, or disorientation with GCS 13-15. High-risk criteria identify patients needing neurosurgical intervention. Medium-risk criteria identify those with brain injury on CT. The rule has 100% sensitivity for identifying need for neurosurgical intervention.

cards.front: What is the difference between neurogenic shock and spinal shock?
cards.back:
Neurogenic shock: hypotension with bradycardia from loss of sympathetic tone below injury level (warm, well-perfused extremities). Spinal shock: transient loss of ALL neurologic function below the injury with areflexia and flaccid paralysis.

Neurogenic shock is hemodynamic, caused by unopposed parasympathetic activity below the injury (usually above T6). It must be distinguished from hemorrhagic shock (tachycardia, cool extremities). Spinal shock resolution is indicated by return of reflexes, most commonly the bulbocavernosus reflex.

cards.front: What are the four incomplete spinal cord syndromes and their classic presentations?
cards.back:
1) Brown-Sequard (hemisection): ipsilateral motor loss + proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temp loss. 2) Anterior cord: bilateral motor + pain/temp loss, preserved proprioception. 3) Central cord (most common): upper > lower extremity weakness. 4) Posterior cord: bilateral proprioception loss, preserved motor + pain/temp.

Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete SCI, typically from hyperextension injury in an elderly patient with cervical stenosis. Brown-Sequard has the best prognosis. Anterior cord syndrome (from anterior spinal artery occlusion) has the worst prognosis among incomplete injuries.

cards.front: At what spinal levels do the most common cervical disc herniations occur, and what nerve roots are affected?
cards.back:
C5-C6 (C6 root, 19%): affects biceps reflex, thumb sensation. C6-C7 (C7 root, 69%): affects triceps reflex, middle finger sensation. In the cervical spine, disc herniations impinge the nerve root at the level BELOW the interspace.

Unlike the lumbar spine where roots exit below the pedicle, cervical roots exit above (e.g., C6 root exits between C5 and C6). Pain worsens with neck extension, ipsilateral rotation, and lateral flexion. 95% improve spontaneously in 4-8 weeks. Surgical indications include intractable pain >3 months or progressive neurological deficit.

cards.front: What distinguishes neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication?
cards.back:
Neurogenic: dermatomal distribution, relieved by postural changes (sitting, lumbar flexion), induced by standing/walking. Vascular: sclerotomal distribution, relieved by simply resting (stopping exercise), associated with diminished pulses.

Neurogenic claudication results from lumbar spinal stenosis with ischemia of nerve roots. The bicycle test helps distinguish: patients with neurogenic claudication cycle longer because the flexed position opens the spinal canal. Clinical exam may be normal, including straight leg raise. MRI is best for confirming stenosis.

cards.front: What is syringomyelia and what is its most common association?
cards.back:
Cystic cavitation of the spinal cord. 70% are associated with Chiari I malformation.

Syringomyelia initially causes pain and weakness, then loss of pain and temperature sensation (spinothalamic tract) in the upper extremities with preserved touch and proprioception (dorsal columns). This 'dissociated sensory loss' is characteristic. Other associations include post-traumatic, tumors, and tethered cord. MRI is the best diagnostic modality.

cards.front: What type of odontoid fracture has the highest risk of non-union?
cards.back:
Type II — fracture through the base of the dens, in the watershed zone of blood supply.

Odontoid fractures are the most common C2 fracture. Type I is an avulsion of the tip (stable). Type II is through the base of the dens (most common, highest non-union risk). Type III extends into the C2 vertebral body (lower non-union risk). Type II fractures more often require surgical fixation.

cards.front: What are the criteria for neurologically determined death (brain death)?
cards.back:
Prerequisites: no CNS depressants, no intoxication, temp >32C, no metabolic derangement. Findings: absent ALL brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, caloric, pharyngeal, cough) and absent respiratory drive at PaCO2 >=60 mmHg (apnea test). Requires 2 evaluations by 2 specialists.

Brain death is irreversible and diffuse brain injury with absence of all clinical brain function. Cardiovascular activity may persist for up to 2 weeks. Confirmatory tests include flat EEG and absent cerebral perfusion on angiogram. This determination has legal implications for organ donation.

cards.front: What is the Spetzler-Martin grading scale for AVMs?
cards.back:
Three components: Size (<3cm=1, 3-6cm=2, >6cm=3), Location (non-eloquent=0, eloquent=1), Venous drainage (superficial=0, deep=1). Total grade I-V determines surgical risk.

AVMs are tangles of abnormal vessels with direct arteriovenous shunts without capillary beds. They present with hemorrhage (40-60%), seizures (50%), and mass effect. Annual bleed risk is 2-4%. Surgical excision is treatment of choice for Spetzler-Martin grades I-II. SRS is preferred for small (<3cm) or deep lesions.

cards.front: What are the red flags for back pain that suggest serious underlying pathology (mnemonic: BACK PAIN)?
cards.back:
B: Bowel/bladder dysfunction. A: Anesthesia (saddle). C: Constitutional symptoms. K: Khronic disease. P: Paresthesia. A: Age >50 or <20. I: IV drug use. N: Neuromotor deficits.

These red flags should prompt urgent investigation. Cauda equina syndrome requires emergent MRI and surgical decompression within 48 hours. Malignancy should be suspected with age >50, history of cancer, and pain unrelieved by bed rest. Infection risk increases with IV drug use, immunosuppression, and elevated ESR.

cards.front: What is the most common type of myelomeningocele-associated brain malformation?
cards.back:
Type II (Arnold-) Chiari malformation, present in 65-85% of myelomeningocele patients.

Myelomeningocele is the most severe common form of spina bifida aperta, involving herniation of meningeal and CNS tissue through a spinal defect. Associated hydrocephalus occurs in 65-85% of patients. Prenatal surgical repair (before 26 weeks) reduces need for CSF shunting from 82% to 40% and improves motor outcomes.

cards.front: What is a CSF fistula, and how is it confirmed?
cards.back:
A communication allowing CSF leak, presenting as otorrhea or rhinorrhea of clear fluid. Confirmed by beta-2 transferrin test (most specific), quantitative glucose analysis, or halo/ring sign.

CSF fistulas occur after head trauma or surgery, or due to high-pressure states. Treatment: lower ICP (avoid straining, acetazolamide), continuous lumbar drainage for persistent leaks. Surgical repair is indicated for leaks lasting >2 weeks, spontaneous leaks, or those complicated by meningitis.

cards.front: What is the Dandy-Walker malformation?
cards.back:
Atresia of the foramina of Magendie and Luschka, causing cystic dilation of the 4th ventricle, agenesis/hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, enlarged posterior fossa, and hydrocephalus (90%).

Dandy-Walker malformation can be detected in utero. Associated anomalies include agenesis of the corpus callosum (17%). Treatment addresses the hydrocephalus, typically with CSF shunting. It should be distinguished from Chiari malformations, which involve herniation of cerebellar structures through the foramen magnum.

cards.front: What is the Papile classification for intraventricular hemorrhage in neonates?
cards.back:
Grade I: germinal matrix hemorrhage only. Grade II: IVH without ventricular dilation. Grade III: IVH with ventricular dilation. Grade IV: IVH with parenchymal hemorrhage.

IVH primarily occurs in preterm infants (<32 weeks, <1500g). 50% occurs within 8 hours of birth, 90% by day 3. Grades I-II have favorable prognosis. Grades III-IV have greatest morbidity/mortality and may require VP shunt for posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Screening is by routine head ultrasound.

cards.front: What are the three components of Cushing's Triad and what does it indicate?
cards.back:
Cushing's Triad consists of: (1) Bradycardia, (2) Hypertension, and (3) Irregular respiratory pattern. It indicates severely raised intracranial pressure (ICP) and is a late, ominous sign of brainstem compression.

Cushing's Triad results from the brainstem's response to critical ischemia when ICP approaches MAP. The body attempts to raise MAP to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP), causing reflex bradycardia via baroreceptors. It is seen in only 1/3 of cases with acutely raised ICP and signifies impending herniation.

cards.front: What is the Monro-Kellie doctrine and why is it clinically important?
cards.back:
The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the brain is encased in a rigid skull with a fixed intracranial volume. The intracranial space contains CSF, blood, and brain parenchyma. An increase in one constituent must be compensated by a decrease in another; once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, ICP rises exponentially.

Understanding this doctrine explains why compensatory reserve exists (60-80 mL in young, 100-140 mL in elderly due to cerebral atrophy). Immediate compensation occurs via egress of CSF through foramen magnum and venous blood displacement. Late stages cause decreased CPP, ischemia, cerebral edema, and herniation. Clinically, elderly patients tolerate more volume expansion before decompensation.

cards.front: What are the ICP thresholds for initiating treatment and for life-threatening emergency?
cards.back:
ICP >25 mmHg: end-organ damage possible, treatment should be initiated. ICP >40 mmHg: life-threatening emergency, urgent pressure reduction required. Normal ICP: 10-15 mmHg in adults, 3-7 mmHg in children, 1.5-6 mmHg in infants.

These thresholds guide neurosurgical management. Treatment targets are ICP <20 mmHg, CPP 60-70 mmHg, and sBP >100 mmHg (ages 50-69) or >110 mmHg (age <50 or >70). Monitoring ICP is indicated in severe TBI (GCS <8) with abnormal CT, or normal CT with two or more of: age >40, BP <90 mmHg, or abnormal motor posturing.

cards.front: What is the gold standard method for ICP measurement and what therapeutic advantage does it offer?
cards.back:
The intraventricular catheter (External Ventricular Drain, EVD) is the gold standard for ICP measurement. Its therapeutic advantage is that it allows drainage of CSF (3-5 mL) to reduce intracranial volume and lower ICP.

Other monitoring options include parenchymal ICP monitors, Licox monitors (intraventricular, intraparenchymal, subdural), subarachnoid bolt (Richmond screw), and epidural monitors. Non-invasive methods (transcranial Doppler, CT/MRI, fundoscopy) are not accurate enough for routine measurement. Serial LP can be used for monitoring but is not the most accurate and is contraindicated in suspected acutely raised ICP or obstructive hydrocephalus.

cards.front: What are the four types of cerebral edema and their mechanisms?
cards.back:
(1) Vasogenic: BBB compromised (meningitis, hypertensive encephalopathy, tumour, late ischemia). (2) Cytotoxic: BBB intact, cell death (early ischemia, brain injury, encephalitis, status epilepticus). (3) Interstitial: transudation of CSF into periventricular white matter in hydrocephalus (transependymal edema). (4) Osmotic: osmotic gradient increases intracellular free H2O (acute hyponatremia, hepatic encephalopathy).

Distinguishing edema type is critical for management. Vasogenic edema responds to dexamethasone (reduces BBB permeability), whereas cytotoxic edema does not. Osmotic edema from acute hyponatremia should not be corrected too rapidly due to risk of central pontine myelinolysis. Interstitial edema resolves with treatment of underlying hydrocephalus.

cards.front: What is cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) and what is its target range in management of elevated ICP?
cards.back:
CPP = MAP - ICP. Normal CPP is >50 mmHg. Treatment targets: CPP 60-70 mmHg. Cerebral autoregulation fails when CPP <40 mmHg or MAP >150 mmHg or <50 mmHg.

Maintaining adequate CPP is essential to prevent secondary brain injury. Cerebral autoregulation normally keeps CBF constant across a range of CPP. In brain injury (e.g., SAH, severe trauma), autoregulation is impaired and CBF becomes pressure-passive. The brain receives approximately 15% of cardiac output (~750 mL/min). Increased CO2 and decreased O2 (<50 mmHg) both cause cerebral vasodilation and increased CBF.

cards.front: Describe the stepwise management of elevated ICP using the ICP HEAD mnemonic.
cards.back:
ICP HEAD: (I)CP — treat primary etiology; (H)ead — elevate head of bed 30° in neutral position; (E)levate — adequate BP (maintain sBP targets); (A)dequate BP — prevent hypotension; (D)iuretic — mannitol or hypertonic saline. Plus: Calm (sedate), Coma (barbiturate-induced), Place drain (EVD), Paralysis (vecuronium), Hyperventilate (pCO2 30-35 mmHg briefly).

The mnemonic helps prioritize interventions. Mannitol 20% IV at 1-1.5 g/kg reduces ICP within 15-30 min by increasing serum tonicity. 3% hypertonic saline is comparable to mannitol. Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic edema around tumours/abscesses but has no proven value in head injury or stroke. Hyperventilation is a temporizing measure only — avoid within 24h of trauma. Decompressive craniectomy is definitive for refractory ICP.

cards.front: What are the 5 types of herniation syndromes and their key clinical features?
cards.back:
(1) Subfalcine: cingulate gyrus under falx — usually asymptomatic, warns of impending transtentorial herniation. (2) Central (tentorial): diencephalon through tentorial notch — small fixed pupils, decreased LOC, sunset eyes. (3) Uncal (lateral tentorial): uncus through tentorial notch — ipsilateral dilated unreactive pupil (earliest sign), CN III palsy, decreased LOC, contralateral hemiplegia. (4) Upward: cerebellar vermis through tentorial incisura — cerebellar infarct, hydrocephalus. (5) Tonsillar: cerebellar tonsils through foramen magnum — neck stiffness, flaccid paralysis, respiratory arrest.

Uncal herniation is the most clinically recognized: the earliest and most reliable sign is an ipsilateral non-reactive dilated pupil due to CN III compression. Kernohan's notch is a false localizing sign where ipsilateral hemiplegia occurs due to the edge of tentorium compressing the contralateral cerebral peduncle. Tonsillar herniation can be precipitated by LP in the presence of an intracranial mass — hence the importance of CT before LP in suspected elevated ICP.

cards.front: What is the earliest and most reliable sign of uncal (lateral tentorial) herniation?
cards.back:
Ipsilateral non-reactive dilated pupil due to compression of CN III (oculomotor nerve), accompanied by ipsilateral EOM paralysis and ptosis.

The uncus of the temporal lobe herniates downward through the tentorial notch, compressing CN III which runs along the edge of the tentorium. CN III carries parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibres on its outer surface, so compression causes a blown pupil (mydriasis) before other signs. This is distinguished from a direct CN III palsy (e.g., from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm), which also presents with a dilated pupil. Decreased LOC follows due to midbrain compression.

cards.front: What is Kernohan's notch and why is it a false localizing sign?
cards.back:
Kernohan's notch is a false localizing sign in uncal herniation where ipsilateral hemiplegia occurs because the edge of the tentorium compresses the contralateral cerebral peduncle. This produces ipsilateral (same side as lesion) rather than expected contralateral weakness.

In uncal herniation, the expected finding is contralateral hemiplegia (corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla). However, when the herniating uncus pushes the brainstem against the opposite tentorial edge, it compresses the contralateral cerebral peduncle — causing ipsilateral motor weakness relative to the mass. This can mislead clinicians about the laterality of the causative lesion. Kernohan's notch is one of the classic false localizing signs in neurosurgery.

cards.front: What is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumour cerebri) and what are the Modified Dandy's Criteria for diagnosis?
cards.back:
IIH is raised ICP with papilledema without mass, hydrocephalus, infection, or hypertensive encephalopathy. Modified Dandy's Criteria: (1) Symptoms of raised ICP; (2) No localizing signs except CN VI palsy; (3) Patient awake and alert; (4) Normal neuroimaging without evidence of mass; (5) LP opening pressure >25 cm H2O with normal CSF; (6) No better explanation for raised ICP.

IIH predominantly affects obese women of childbearing age (incidence 19-21/100,000/yr in this group vs. 1-2/100,000/yr general population). Risk factors overlap with venous sinus thrombosis ('fat, female, fertile, forties'). Associated causes include hypervitaminosis A, steroid withdrawal, tetracycline, amiodarone, lithium, oral contraceptives, growth hormone, and retinoids. CN VI palsy is an exception to the 'no localizing signs' criterion due to CN VI's long intracranial course making it vulnerable to ICP changes.

cards.front: Which medications must be used with caution in elevated ICP and why?
cards.back:
Nitroprusside: raises ICP via direct arterial vasodilation (arterial > venous) → increased cerebral blood volume. Nitroglycerin: raises ICP via vasodilation but less so (venous > arterial). Succinylcholine: induced fasciculations may transiently increase ICP.

These drugs are commonly used in critical care but can worsen intracranial hypertension. Nitroprusside is of particular concern in neurosurgical patients with mass lesions. When blood pressure control is needed, agents with less effect on cerebral vasculature are preferred. Succinylcholine's ICP-raising effect is generally mild and brief, but alternatives (rocuronium) are preferred in refractory ICP situations.

cards.front: What are the consequences of a lesion in each major brain region: frontal lobe, parietal lobe (dominant vs. non-dominant), temporal lobe, and occipital lobe?
cards.back:
Frontal lobe: abulia, disinhibition, apathy, executive dysfunction, + primitive reflexes, contralateral UMN signs. Parietal lobe (dominant/left): aphasias, Gerstmann's syndrome. Parietal lobe (non-dominant/right): hemispatial neglect, apraxias, agnosias. Temporal lobe: hippocampus → anterograde amnesia; upper homonymous hemianopia; Wernicke's aphasia (left). Occipital lobe: contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

Gerstmann's syndrome (dominant parietal) includes acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation. Broca's area (posterior inferior frontal gyrus, dominant): non-fluent aphasia, impaired repetition, spared comprehension. Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, dominant): fluent aphasia, impaired repetition and comprehension. Non-dominant parietal also causes dressing apraxia and cortical sensory loss. These localization patterns are high-yield for MCCQE1.

cards.front: What is Broca's aphasia and how does it differ from Wernicke's aphasia?
cards.back:
Broca's aphasia (posterior inferior frontal gyrus, dominant hemisphere): non-fluent, dysarthric speech; impaired repetition; comprehension spared. Wernicke's aphasia (posterior superior temporal gyrus, dominant hemisphere): fluent but paraphasic speech; impaired repetition; comprehension impaired.

Broca's area is typically in the left inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44, 45). Damage produces effortful, telegraphic speech with preserved comprehension — patients are often distressed by their deficit. Wernicke's area is in the posterior superior temporal gyrus; damage produces fluent but meaningless speech (jargon aphasia) with poor comprehension — patients are often unaware of the deficit. Both have impaired repetition, distinguishing them from transcortical aphasias.

cards.front: What are the consequences of brainstem lesions at different levels?
cards.back:
Dorsal midbrain (pineal gland): Parinaud's syndrome (supranuclear upward gaze palsy). Pons: locked-in syndrome. Below red nucleus (midbrain): decerebrate posture. Above red nucleus: decorticate posture. CPA (cerebellopontine angle): disequilibrium, ataxia, CN V/VII/VIII deficits. Reticular activating system (midbrain): reduced level of arousal.

Parinaud's syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome) classically occurs with pinealoma or hydrocephalus compressing the tectum — features include upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and lid retraction. Locked-in syndrome (bilateral ventral pontine infarct) spares consciousness but causes quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved vertical gaze. Decorticate posturing (flexion of arms, extension of legs) indicates a lesion above the red nucleus; decerebrate (extension of all limbs) indicates a lesion below.

cards.front: What is the frontal eye field rule for gaze deviation in frontal vs. cortical lesions?
cards.back:
Destructive lesion of frontal eye fields: gaze deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion (eyes look at the lesion). Irritative lesion (e.g., seizure): gaze deviates AWAY from the irritative focus.

The frontal eye fields (FEF, Brodmann area 8) normally drive conjugate eye movements to the contralateral side. A destructive lesion removes this drive, so the intact contralateral FEF pushes gaze toward the lesion side ('looking at the stroke'). During a focal seizure, the FEF is hyperactive, driving gaze contralaterally — away from the irritative focus ('looking away from the seizure'). This distinction is useful in localizing acute stroke vs. seizure activity.

cards.front: What are the consequences of cerebellar hemisphere vs. cerebellar vermis lesions?
cards.back:
Cerebellar hemisphere: intention tremor, ipsilateral limb ataxia (SAME side as lesion), fall toward the side of lesion. Cerebellar vermis: truncal ataxia, dysarthria.

Cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral deficits because the cerebellum controls the ipsilateral side of the body (double decussation of motor pathways). Hemisphere lesions affect limb coordination (finger-nose ataxia, heel-shin ataxia), while vermis lesions affect axial coordination (gait and truncal balance) and speech. Fall toward the lesion side is a classic exam finding. DASHING mnemonic for cerebellar signs: Dysdiadochokinesis, Ataxia, Slurred speech, Hypotonia, Intention tremor, Nystagmus, Gait disturbance.

cards.front: What are the indications for ICP monitoring in severe TBI?
cards.back:
ICP monitoring is indicated for: (1) Severe TBI (GCS <8T) with abnormal CT scan. (2) Severe TBI with normal CT if two or more of: age >40, BP <90 mmHg, abnormal motor posturing. ('T' in GCS <8T refers to intubation, tracheostomy, or factors affecting verbal response.)

These indications are based on Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines. An abnormal CT includes SAH, hematoma, contusion, basal cistern compression, swelling, and herniation with GCS <8. ICP monitoring guides management of CPP, guides diuretic use, and determines need for surgical decompression. EVD remains gold standard as it allows therapeutic CSF drainage in addition to monitoring.

cards.front: What is the approach to time of onset in intracranial pathology (vascular vs. metabolic vs. infectious vs. tumour)?
cards.back:
Vascular: sudden onset (occlusive = no headache; hemorrhagic = headache). Metabolic: hours to days, affects entire CNS. Infectious: days to weeks, often with source of infection or immunodeficiency on history.
